video:video.video:title: 24-7PressRelease Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Every release is paid separately, from $29 to $479, and the pricing page describes each plan in a single line; the comparison page linked from it returned 'Page Not Found' when we read it. The $29 Simple Post is not distribution at all, only a post on their own site, and only the $479 plan names PR Newswire. A wire release puts your text in front of outlets; it does not guarantee coverage. We have not sent a release through 24-7PressRelease ourselves.

video:video.video:title: AISDR Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Judge it on cost per meeting, not the sticker. Pay as you go at $1.50 per person contacted removes the old entry barrier, but the bill grows with every person you contact, so a weak list costs you money as well as sender reputation. Autonomous AI outreach is only as good as your targeting, list quality and messaging guardrails; point it at a bad list and you'll automate bad outreach. For teams with a solid ICP and offer it can book meetings at a real cost per meeting; for those still figuring out messaging, it's premature. Ami, the GTM agent AiSDR shipped in September 2026, is now the front door on every route: you hand it your website, it comes back with a target list and a campaign, and it keeps adjusting the ones that stall, with your ICP, exclusions and past lessons carried over between campaigns. The scale numbers on the launch page (17,150 campaigns learned from, 19,501 meetings behind them, a rolling 30-day pipeline counter) are AiSDR's own and unaudited, so read them as marketing rather than evidence. And Ami changes none of the deliverability arithmetic: a first campaign in minutes is the launch, not the result.

video:video.video:title: AISQ Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: AISQ (the Squirrly family) evolves its pricing and product names often — the honest advice is to buy only what's currently priced in front of you, in small credit batches first, and judge output on YOUR niche keywords before committing to bundles. Marketing automation that promises to cut workload 90% still needs your strategy and editing; credits generate drafts, not customers.

video:video.video:title: AdCreative.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The meter counts downloads, not campaigns — iterate seriously on ad variations and a 10-credit starter evaporates in an afternoon, which is exactly what iteration-heavy ad work does. And the honest fundamental: AI creatives give you volume and speed, but the offer and the hook still decide performance — a mediocre offer with 500 AI banners is 500 mediocre banners. Size the credit tier to your real testing cadence.

video:video.video:title: AgencyAnalytics Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Cost scales linearly with clients — great at 5, pricey at 50+. The most-cited complaint is connector reliability: data sources disconnect and the platform doesn't always flag the failure clearly. Solo or small-data setups get little value from it.

video:video.video:title: AgentNest Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Two months old and still no reviews. The app launched on 6 August 2026; on 9 October 2026 the listing still showed zero reviews, which is not a criticism so much as the plain state of the evidence. Everything below is read off the listing, because there is nothing else to read.
The score is the vendor's own. 'AI shopping readiness' is measured by AgentNest against AgentNest's criteria, and no external standard — no schema.org profile, no Google Merchant Center specification, no published rubric — is named anywhere on the listing. A number that only one company calculates is a prompt to go look at your catalogue, not a fact about your catalogue. On the same page Shopify shows ListingLens and StoreBeam doing the same job, also on free plans.
And the billing unit is defined by the party doing the billing. You pay per 'successful automated fix', with no definition of a fix and no definition of successful. Combined with permissions that let it edit products, collections and files across your store, the sensible way in is: run the free scan, read the issue list, fix a handful yourself, and only then decide whether the one-click version is worth 19 cents a go. The same developer's other app, AskNest, has one review in three months — this is a two-app studio finding its feet, not an established catalogue tool.

video:video.video:title: Aira Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Young product, sharp focus: European B2B prospecting on a 65-million-company database with meeting notes flowing into records automatically. The honest checks: independent review coverage is still thin, so run your own two-week test against a concrete metric (meetings booked, admin hours saved) rather than trusting early-adopter buzz. And note that the money-back guarantee exists precisely so you can do that without risk.

video:video.video:title: AltText.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The headline ‘5¢ per image’ only holds for a plain JPG in one language. AVIF, HEIC, SVG and TIFF bill double — precisely the formats a performance-tuned image pipeline outputs — and every extra language adds another credit per image, so by the published rules one AVIF product shot in five languages is six credits, not one. Those advanced formats are also locked out of the 25-credit free trial, so the one thing you cannot measure before paying is your own burn rate. In our test on 20 October 2026 the free upload form refused an AVIF with 'Please choose a JPG, PNG, or WebP image.' before charging a credit, and plain JPG and PNG images cost 1 credit each. With English and Dutch both selected we got only a Dutch text for 1 credit, so check what a multi-language run returns before you budget for one. Credits are spent on generation rather than on acceptance: regenerate a line you didn’t like and you pay again, and AltText.ai states plainly that used credits are not normally refundable. The category caveat an honest review owes you: models describe what is visibly in a photo well, but alt text is a judgement call. Whether an image is decorative or informative, and what your brand actually calls the thing in it, is context the model doesn’t have. Bulk generation is a far better starting point than the empty alt attributes on most sites, but treat the output as a draft to spot-check. ‘ADA compliance’ here means the field gets filled, not a legal guarantee that what’s in it is right.

video:video.video:title: Amplemarket Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's premium and built for teams that will use the whole all-in-one stack. The independent picture is genuinely strong overall: around 4.6/5 across ~600 G2 reviews, with repeated praise for unusually human-sounding AI messages, ease of use and hands-on support. But data accuracy and email deliverability are the most-cited complaints, and they cluster on European contacts — North American data holds up better than EMEA/APAC. Amplemarket points to its own benchmarks showing competitive accuracy, so weigh both sides and test their data against your own target region in a trial before you commit. Under ~10 reps you'll also pay for features you never touch. The genuinely new bit: it now works inside ChatGPT and Claude. Since June that integration can triage the inbox and update or remove leads rather than just search, so reps can run more of the workflow without leaving the chat. Since July that stretches further. From the same chat a rep can research an account, pull enriched profiles and enrol every contact into one sequence with copy written per person and per step. A GTM Skills Library exposes the rest of the platform the same way. Amplemarket says setup takes under two minutes — that is their figure, not one we timed.

video:video.video:title: Assortion Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The price follows your total store orders, so you pay the same whether the upsells sell or not, and busy months can push you into the next tier. App blocks only work on product pages. We found no refund or cancellation policy, and the page does not say how refunded orders or a tier change mid-month are handled.

video:video.video:title: Atlas AI Store Builder Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The meter runs on your success, not your usage. $1,000 of bundle revenue and 250 cart orders is a rounding error for a store that is actually working. So the $39 headline describes the bill of a store that has not started selling yet. Price the tier you expect to be on in month three, not the one you sign up on. Two other things worth knowing before you install. The rating is 4.6 from 374 reviews on 9 October 2026, but 25 of those are one star and the recent ones are about billing rather than the product: one seller writes “cancelled it, uninstalled it, but still getting charged” after two months. And the listing carries a line Shopify does not require of most apps: “Atlas must not be used to copy, duplicate, or reproduce products, product listings, images, or store content from any website, or marketplace without the explicit permission of the rights holder”. That tells you what a paste-a-product-link builder gets used for.

video:video.video:title: Atria Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two honest notes. It's credit-metered — AI credits and brand-tracking slots cap what you can generate and monitor, so a heavy user burns through Core's allowance and steps up to Plus. And it's specialized for Meta/TikTok ad creative research and generation, so it's a performance-marketing tool, not a general design suite. Its edge is competitor ad intelligence plus creative generation in one place; if you only need one of those, a cheaper single-purpose tool may fit.

video:video.video:title: Attribuly Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pricing has moved within two months. In August and September 2026 the listing went from free straight to $450 or $500 a month; on 14 October 2026 the recovery plan, ReCapture, had become a $100 monthly minimum plus 10% of the incremental revenue it recovers, while Capture stayed at $450 flat. The new shape lowers the entry cost but ties the bill to a figure Attribuly itself measures, so ask how 'incremental' is deduplicated against your existing Klaviyo flows before the trial ends. It is still an add-on rather than a replacement: the pitch is explicitly that it recovers carts “Klaviyo misses” and syncs identity signals back into Klaviyo, so you pay for this on top of an email platform you already pay for.

video:video.video:title: Aura Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The tier is decided by how much you sell, not by what you need. That is unusually honest as a model — a seller doing $10K a month is not subsidising one doing $900K — but it means your bill moves when your business does, in the same month, without you choosing to upgrade. Pass $15K and Starter stops being the plan you are on. Work out which band you land in the way the page measures it: their table says monthly sales are calculated on a trailing two months, so it is a sustained climb rather than a single spike that moves you up. Two smaller things: the marketplace count is a real cap (two on Starter, so Amazon plus one), and the AI listing allowance is per listing rather than per repricing action, so a large catalogue eats it faster than a busy one.

video:video.video:title: AutoWrite Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest thing to say about this one is that there is nothing to judge yet: on 18 August 2026 the App Store listing showed a rating of 0.0 from zero reviews, and on 9 October 2026 it still did. Not one merchant has publicly reported using it. That is not a criticism of the product, it is a statement about the evidence — an AI blog writer that nobody has reviewed is a bet, and it should be priced as one. The category it sits in is also crowded with tools that have years of track record behind them.

video:video.video:title: Auware Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's deliberately narrow — Shopify-only and built around segmented paid traffic. If you send everyone to one page or don't run audience-segmented ads, the core 'a page per persona' value doesn't really kick in. It's also newer and less battle-tested than general builders like PageFly.

video:video.video:title: Ava AI Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The monthly price is a minutes allowance, not a flat fee — every minute past the bucket bills at $0.07 to $0.10, so a busy support line can cost far more than the headline. And keep the vendor's marketing at arm's length: Ava launched in September 2025 with just six App Store reviews, and the promoted 21–24x ROAS figures are the vendor's own, not independently verified. There is no free plan, only a 7-day trial.

video:video.video:title: Beefree Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Read the seat row before the price row. Professional and Business both cap at two full editing seats, so a "mid-sized team" plan at $134/mo annual still buys two people who can actually build. Everyone else lands in view-only slots — four on Professional, ten on Business — or an Enterprise quote. The free Starter is the odd one out: unlimited users, but with no roles or permissions at all. Exports are metered at six a month, rather than the unlimited free tier its old reputation suggests, and in our test on 21 October 2026 merely showing the HTML code used one of them (6 left became 5). And the naming is a live tripwire. Since 14 May 2026 the builder is RGE Studio at reallygoodemails.com, while Beefree remains the company name and the name of the separate developer SDK. So check which product a plan or invoice actually refers to. It is purely a creation environment that never sends, so it always sits on top of your ESP. Worth it when the ESP's native editor is the bottleneck — agencies, multi-brand teams, ESP migrations — and duplicated effort when it isn't.

video:video.video:title: Beehiiv Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Next to Substack it's more to learn. Substack's built-in discovery network and dead-simple setup are easier if you're starting from zero with no audience and don't care about automation or SEO. Beehiiv's depth is the point, but it's a steeper start.

video:video.video:title: BidX Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The number that decides your bill is the one number the page does not print. Every Amazon PPC and DSP tier ends with “+ % of connected ad spend per month”, and that percentage appears nowhere — not on the tier cards, not in the footnotes, not in the FAQ. So €495 is a floor, not a price, and nobody spending real money on Amazon ads can work out their monthly cost from this page. Ask for the percentage in writing, and ask whether it is charged on all connected spend or only on what BidX manages, before you get as far as a contract.
The second thing to price is the commitment. The page states plans run on an annual commitment paid monthly, and the FAQ confirms it: the commitment is annual, and the only shorter path on offer is a paid three-month proof of concept. There is no free trial. That makes the cheapest visible door €5,940 a year net of VAT before a cent of the percentage — a very different proposition from the €495 the eye lands on.
Two smaller inconsistencies worth noticing, because they tell you how carefully the price list is maintained. On a page priced in euros, the one add-on with a hard number is quoted in dollars ($250 per extra 500 keywords), so ask which currency you are actually billed in. And BidX Essential — the $195/month product they route smaller sellers to — lives on a completely separate landing page carrying a 2024 copyright line and a different phone number. It is not listed among the tiers on the pricing page itself, so confirm it still exists at that price before you plan around it.

video:video.video:title: Birch Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest catch is that pricing tracks your ad spend, so a scaling advertiser's bill rises with their budget: Pro alone ladders from $99 to $1,799 a month between a $10,000 and a $500,000 ceiling, and past $500,000 only Enterprise is left. Check the annual arithmetic yourself: the toggle advertises ‘-20%’, but the page charges eleven months — $540 for Essential and $1,090 for Pro at the entry tier, about 8% off. It's also a power tool: rule-based automation across Meta, Google, TikTok and Snapchat rewards advertisers who know what to automate, and can amplify mistakes if your rules are wrong. For hands-on performance marketers, it's a serious time-saver.

video:video.video:title: Bitscale Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The free tier is real and needs no card, which makes Bitscale unusually easy to judge for yourself before paying. What to check during that trial is not the feature list but your own burn rate, and Bitscale's credit table tells you the range in advance: one to twelve credits for every email or phone the waterfall finds, depending on how many providers you let it try. That is the whole budget question. The same 15,000 credits on Growth are 15,000 enriched contacts at one credit and 1,250 at twelve, so the plan you buy matters less than the depth you configure. Run fifty real records on the free 200 credits, read the meter before and after, and multiply by your monthly volume -- that number, not the plan price, is your bill.
One free-tier number is worth holding against the other. The plan table gives Free a 50,000-row grid, while Bitscale's own onboarding mail says the free plan scores up to 200 rows at a time -- and both are true, because a Score column, which grades every row against an ideal-customer profile you describe in plain English, is an AI enrichment at one to two credits a run. The grid is not the ceiling, the 200 credits are. Finding the names draws on the separate pool of 2,000 search credits, so building the list is the cheap half; asking the product to judge it is the half that runs out.

video:video.video:title: Bold Custom Pricing Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Bold Custom Pricing has no free plan and charges by customer group: a second price list already takes you from $29 to $69 a month, and bulk CSV pricing and the Shopify POS integration sit only on Complete at $129. The reviews are split more sharply than the 4.4 suggests, with 58 of 538 at one star. The recent complaints are specific: price syncing that broke and 'wreaked havoc' (October 2026, fixed by support), crashes for three weeks with no answer from support (June 2026), incorrect pricing that cost more than the app (February 2026), a slower store and order numbers disturbed while support removed the app (February 2026), and ten days of changing cart quantities and wrong prices after migrating to the new version (April 2025). We have not run the app ourselves; this dossier is read from the listing and its reviews.

video:video.video:title: Bold Memberships Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Bold Memberships charges for every member, every month: $0.13 each after the first 10, so a free loyalty tier with 10,000 customers costs about $1,300 a month, and the listing does not say whether free members count. Paid tiers run through Stripe rather than Shopify's checkout; a January 2026 review notes that sign-ups do not appear as Shopify orders. The newest reviews are warm about support, but the 1- and 2-star reviews describe member tags vanishing and customers locked out (2021, 2022), members still charged after the app was deleted (2022), and a 2022 complaint about compatibility with modern themes. The data access is wide, including viewing sensitive customer data and editing orders and store credit. We have not run the app ourselves; this dossier is read from the listing, Bold's product page and the reviews.

video:video.video:title: Bold Subscriptions Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Bold Subscriptions never stops charging a percentage. Every plan adds a transaction fee of 0.9% to 2% on top of the monthly price, so the bill grows with your subscription revenue: at $30,000 a month it is about $350 even on the best plan. The higher plans buy nothing but that lower fee, and all three list the same standard support. The recent reviews we read are uneven: praise for chat support sits beside a merchant double-charged for nearly three years after a version merge (June 2026), a store down for 48 hours after an app update with no refund offered (February 2026), and a week without an answer to support emails (May 2026). The data access is wide, including viewing sensitive customer data and editing orders. We have not run the app ourselves; this dossier is read from the listing and its reviews.

video:video.video:title: Bold Upsell Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Bold Upsell is priced by your Shopify plan, so a store on Shopify Advanced pays $74.99 a month for exactly the feature list a Basic store gets for $4.99, and checkout offers need Shopify Plus at $399.99 a month. The 7-day trial is short for judging an upsell app. The reviews are mostly warm, but 50 of 594 are one- or two-star, and the recent ones are specific: add-to-cart and checkout rates down 70% after offers went live (January 2026), the app failing at its one job with support silent for days or weeks (edited October 2026), and the app stopping without notice (November 2025). The data access is wide, including viewing sensitive customer data and editing orders and discounts. We have not run the app ourselves; this dossier is read from the listing and its reviews.

video:video.video:title: Bot It AI Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The budget behind the AI fixes is not published. Pro's automated fixes draw on a monthly token budget the vendor describes only as generous. Its FAQ puts a typical product at about a thousand tokens to enrich once and says the app stops proposing, never mid-write, when you reach the ceiling. For a catalogue of a few hundred products that is unlikely to matter. For tens of thousands of SKUs, or for re-enriching after every catalogue change, ask for the number in writing before you rely on it.
It is a bet on a channel that is still small. The app prepares your catalogue for AI shopping agents, including ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Claude, and tracks where your products place in their results. For most stores those agents are not yet a meaningful source of orders, so the rank tracker and the agent-traffic analytics may show very little for a while. The audit is useful regardless, because the fields it checks (categories, attributes, barcodes, alt text, variants, policies) also feed shopping feeds and on-site search.
Nobody has reviewed it yet. The app launched on the Shopify App Store on 8 May 2026 and still had zero reviews on 24 September 2026, so there is no outside account of how accurate its generated attributes are. Start in Full Review mode, where every proposal waits for your approval, before you let Full Auto write to your live catalogue.

video:video.video:title: Brandye Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Read the free plan as a trial, not a tier. Its 100 quiz submissions and 100 chats are lifetime totals, not monthly, so a store with real traffic uses them up in days or weeks and then has to pay. Data retention is the other quiet limit: the free plan keeps 15 days of data and Starter 30, so the quiz answers and chat history you would use to spot patterns over a season are only kept for 90 days on Growth at $129 a month or above.
The Shopify listing shows four plans and stops at $129. The vendor's own pricing page goes on to Scale at $249 and Brand at $599 a month, so a growing store that reads only the listing will not see where the ladder ends. The listing also gives English as the only language, while 11 of its 12 reviews come from French stores and are written in French, so check how the quiz and assistant handle your shoppers' language before you rely on them.
The reviews are uniformly positive but say little that can be checked. Most praise the team as much as the app, naming the founder and describing hands-on help with installing and customising the quiz, and several were written after days or weeks of use. One says conversion went up and returns went down, without figures. The homepage figures of a 16% higher average order value and five times the conversion rate are, by Brandye's own footnote, indicative midpoints of its reported ranges, not measurements we can verify. Brandye's legal page lists quiz responses among the data it collects and says collected data is used, among other things, for marketing and retargeting campaigns; it does not say whether that covers your shoppers' answers or only visitors to brandye.com, so ask before you install if that matters to you. We have not installed the app.

video:video.video:title: CallRail Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The headline price is a floor, not a ceiling — the included minutes, numbers and SMS are modest, so an active campaign quickly hits metered overages that meaningfully lift the bill. It's also specifically an attribution tool: it proves which marketing drives calls and leads, but it isn't a phone system or CRM, so you add it alongside those, not instead of them.

video:video.video:title: Campaign Monitor Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: You pay for contacts, not sends — so a large, quiet list costs the same as a large, active one, and dormant subscribers are literally a line item. Clean your list before comparing prices anywhere. Campaign Monitor's strength is polished, agency-friendly email; its automation depth is lighter than dedicated marketing-automation platforms, so know which of the two jobs you're actually buying.

video:video.video:title: Campaigner Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two paragraphs of fine print worth reading. Automation workflows and conversion tracking only arrive on Advanced (from $35 a month at 1,000 contacts) — Essentials is a sending tool with an API, not a marketing-automation platform — and the trial auto-converts to paid if you do not actively cancel, which tells you something about the retention strategy. Contact-based pricing also means dormant subscribers bill like active ones; prune first.

video:video.video:title: Capsule Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Capsule's simplicity is the product: it deliberately does less than the CRM giants, which is why small teams actually use it. The honest flip side — advanced automation, deep reporting and integrations thin out at the top tiers, and a scaling sales org can outgrow it. Buy it to finally have a CRM the team fills in; plan a migration path if you're heading toward enterprise process complexity.

video:video.video:title: CarouselBot Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Free exports carry a watermark and the free card sets, batch and document are lifetime totals, not monthly. Creator allows only 3 batches a month. The refund window is 7 days, the cards do not name their currency, and Business is only a starting price.

video:video.video:title: Circle Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The sticker is only the entry: Circle keeps a commission on every sale on top of Stripe's processing fees, and email marketing is a separate add-on — so a monetized community's real bill runs meaningfully past the plan price. Model it at your actual sales volume before choosing a tier.

video:video.video:title: Claap Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The four tiers sell two different products, and only one of them is self-serve. Pro at €24 is the recorder and note-taker. Everything Claap actually markets itself on — CRM auto-complete, AI coaching, deal insights, asking Claap AI a question across all your meetings — starts at Business, €48 per license a month on annual billing, and Business has no self-serve button: it says Book a demo. The pricing FAQ closes the other door too: a trial of Pro or Business is opened by their sales team. So the features you came for cannot be bought or tested without a sales conversation.
Your recordings also expire. Storage runs 3 months on Basic, 2 years on Pro and 3 years on Business; only Enterprise is unlimited. If the call archive is meant to be your evidence trail, that is a deletion date on your own data, and it is in the comparison table rather than in the plan cards.
Two smaller things worth reading twice, and one correction we owe you. The AI credits — 500 per license on Pro, 1,000 on Business, pooled across the workspace — do not meter the summaries: the tooltip is explicit that summaries, chapters and the AI companion use no credits, and a credit is spent on a Claap AI chat, an AI email follow-up, the coaching tab or a generated insight. What is missing is the rate: no price for an extra credit appears anywhere on the page, so a heavy month of coaching and insights cannot be costed before you commit. And the free tier's 300 minutes is a total, not a monthly allowance: it is a sample, not a plan you can sit on.

video:video.video:title: Clay Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two honest catches: a steep learning curve (expect 2–4 weeks, many teams need a dedicated Clay expert), and credits that are hard to forecast at scale. It's an enrichment engine, not a sender — you still need Instantly, Lemlist or Outreach to actually email.

video:video.video:title: Cloro Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free tier is a sampler, not a trial of the real thing: 500 credits is about 100 async ChatGPT answers at the 5-credit rate we were actually charged, and their table lists 7 for a full response. Fewer, if you call it synchronously -- and one concurrent job means you queue. Anyone running a daily visibility check across a hundred keywords burns through it in about two days. Read the credit table before the price table -- the same $100 buys 250,000 credits, which is 35,700 full ChatGPT calls or 62,500 Perplexity ones, so your engine mix decides your bill more than your plan does. And nothing carries: their FAQ, read 17 September 2026, states that unused credits expire at the end of every cycle, so a quiet month is money gone rather than headroom for a busy one.

video:video.video:title: Close Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The built-in calling is the draw, but call and SMS credits stack on top of the seat price — a '$99' plan can effectively cost ~$160/user once a rep dials 50+ times a day. Great for call-heavy teams, pricey if you barely dial.

video:video.video:title: Code Bulk Discounts Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Read the free plan's number twice, because the word doing the work is 'lifetime': it is 500 codes in total, not 500 a month. One influencer drop or one email segment can spend the whole allowance in an afternoon, and after that the only way on is $14.99 a month — so the free tier is a sample, not a plan. What the app does is also narrower than the word 'discounts' suggests. It takes a discount you have already created and multiplies it into unique codes you export as a CSV. It does not create the discount rule, does not send the codes to anyone, and does not report which ones were redeemed, so it sits between your discount settings and your email or SMS tool and needs both of those to be worth anything. The one critical review on the listing shows what that costs in practice: when a merchant's parent discount broke after an unrelated change to their stack, every code generated from it went inactive and they learned about it from customers rather than from the app. The developer's answer is the right one to remember — the rules and logic belong to the parent discount, not to Code Bulk — but it means nothing in this app will tell you that a batch has stopped working. The 5.0 rating also rests on 41 reviews, read 16 September 2026, which is a thin record next to the app's peers.

video:video.video:title: Cognism Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: No price, no credit allowance, and a five-seat minimum on both named plans. That combination means the smallest deal is five seats of something you cannot price, so budget conversations start with a sales call rather than a number. The credit model is the part to nail down: one credit reveals one contact, so your real cost per usable lead is the credit price divided by your connect rate, and neither figure is published. Before the call, work out how many contacts a month you actually reveal — that is the only number that lets you judge the quote you get. And it is worth asking whether unused credits roll over, because nothing on the page says.

video:video.video:title: Consentmo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Read the ladder before you budget $10 for this. The two things the listing leads with — web accessibility and a smart region-specific banner — are not on Standard; they start at Plus, $37 a month, which is 3.7 times the entry price. A Shopify Plus store that wants a banner on the checkout needs Enterprise at $64, and so does anything headless or on Hydrogen. The accessibility side is a widget and a scanner: it overlays controls and flags issues, but it does not change the theme markup underneath, which is where an accessibility audit actually looks — treat it as a first layer, not as a remediation. And the free tier puts Consentmo's own branding on the banner your visitors see first.

video:video.video:title: Crazy Egg Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The entry plan is thin on recordings — 50 a month against Hotjar's far more generous free tier. And A/B testing is not in it at all: that starts on Plus at $99, which jumps straight to 150,000 pageviews. Heatmaps need manual per-page setup and annual-only billing locks you in. Like all these tools it's diagnostic — it shows what's broken, it doesn't fix it. Worth knowing before you treat a result as banked: Crazy Egg states it can run A/B tests “after implementing just a small code snippet directly on the website”, which means a winning variant is served by that snippet rather than written into your pages. Stop paying and the original page is what visitors get. Move the winner into your own templates once a test settles.

video:video.video:title: Diginius Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: All-in-one marketing dashboards live or die on data depth per module. Diginius bundles PPC, SEO, lead intelligence and reporting affordably, but specialists — a dedicated SEO suite, a dedicated PPC optimizer — go deeper in their lanes. So buy it as consolidation for a lean team, not as a replacement for expert-grade tooling in your primary channel. Verify the integrations you depend on (especially Microsoft Ads, its historical strength) in the trial.

video:video.video:title: Dondy Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The free plan is a chat button. It is a decent chat button, and conversations through it are unlimited. But none of the marketing this app is named for is in it. Automated cart recovery, campaigns and the official API begin at $79.99 a month, and the $6.99 tier in between only lets you send those same messages by hand.
You will also get two bills. Dondy charges the subscription; Meta charges per conversation on the WhatsApp Business API. Dondy can only tell you the rate starts at $0.0158 or $0.0126, because the real figure depends on the country you are messaging and the type of conversation. A thousand one-click messages a month are included on the two top tiers; past that, your monthly total is not knowable from this listing, and a campaign to a large segment is exactly the kind of thing that produces a surprise. Model it against your own list size and destination countries before you send one.
The rest is Meta's rulebook, not Dondy's. Opt-in, message templates and sender quality are governed on WhatsApp's side, so approval and reach are not things this app can promise you whatever you pay it. The review record is strong — 823 reviews, 92% at the top rating, and the 21 one-star reports have not grown while 49 reviews were added since August — and a misfired broadcast on this channel is still a block rather than an unsubscribe.

video:video.video:title: Drip Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The word “unlimited” quietly expires. At the prices most small shops pay, the send allowance really is uncapped. But the switch has an exact address: unlimited holds to 30,000 people, and from 30,001 the bullet becomes a hard number — 390,000 sends there, 600,000 at 50,000 people, twelve per contact per month. Drip never flags the switch. If you run a daily-deal or high-frequency list, do the arithmetic before you migrate: twelve sends per contact is generous for a monthly newsletter and tight for anything that mails several times a week. The second thing to price in is service. The card looks the same at every level, but two lines on it are not: you cannot talk to anyone in chat until $99/month, and free migration and personalized onboarding only appear from 15,001 people ($249). Below those thresholds it is email support and your own move, which is a real difference on the day a broken automation is sending to the wrong segment.

video:video.video:title: Dripify Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Understand what you are buying before the price matters: LinkedIn prohibits this entire product category. Its User Agreement bans using 'bots or other unauthorized automated methods' to 'send or redirect messages', and its prohibited-software page says members using such tools 'risk having their accounts restricted or shut down'. There is no carve-out for cloud tools or low volumes, and Dripify is not an outlier here — every competitor sits on the same side of that line. Dripify's own documentation is candid about the consequence, warning that LinkedIn 'may issue warnings, temporary restrictions, or even permanent bans', and it publishes a recovery procedure for exactly that scenario. Two things follow. First, the advertised ceiling is not a working speed: the app allows up to 75 connection requests a day, while Dripify's own setup guide tells beginners to run 10 to 15, and brand-new accounts 2 to 5, building up 10 to 20 percent a week. Anyone buying on the headline number is buying capacity they are told not to use. Second, Activity Control sits on the $79 Advanced tier. It is the feature Dripify names as its best protection, and it adjusts your pace automatically. On Basic and Pro, safe pacing is your own manual responsibility. And when a vendor writes that a feature 'makes sure your LinkedIn account won't get flagged', read that as a claim about a third party's enforcement decisions that no vendor can actually guarantee.

video:video.video:title: Dripshipper Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Read the ladder before you climb it. Starter already carries unlimited orders, unlimited products and automatic fulfilment — the whole product, in other words. Professional at $99 adds live monthly training, priority support and a success manager; Elite at $197 adds monthly one-on-one coaching on top. You are buying people, not capability: nothing above Starter makes the coffee ship faster or cost less per bag. The annual rate is the move worth noticing in the other direction, since $240 a year against $30 a month is a third off the same tier. Beyond that the model is narrow by design — one product category, roasted and shipped from their own US facilities in 3-5 business days, with no route to source elsewhere or negotiate the per-order cost.

video:video.video:title: DropGenius Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: We have to be blunt here: the dominant theme in DropGenius’s public buyer reviews is unauthorised charges continuing after cancellation with no route to a refund, and some reviewers report never reaching a dashboard to cancel at all, with support emails bouncing back undeliverable. An AI-generated store in 30 seconds is also just a starting template — the product selection, marketing and margins remain entirely your problem. If you proceed: pay attention to cancellation mechanics from day one, screenshot everything, and treat the Renewal Radar as mandatory equipment.

video:video.video:title: Easy Advanced Translations Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The 'free AI' is quota-limited — 50 products on Free, up to 3,000 on Pro — and past the quota the paid plans bill pay-as-you-go (with a spend limit), so a large multilingual catalogue costs more than the sticker price, or pushes you to your own OpenAI/DeepSeek key, where you pay token costs separately on top of the subscription. Auto-translation of new or changed content is reserved for the higher plans. And the track record is thin: 5.0 stars but only nine reviews, the app launched in July 2025, and it carries no 'Built for Shopify' badge — cheap and promising, but unproven.

video:video.video:title: Easy Bundles Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pricing is tied to the thing the app is supposed to grow. A revenue meter reads as generous at the bottom — $500 of bundle sales a month free is a real trial, not a crippled one — but it means every tier upgrade is triggered by the app working, and the published ladder stops at $10,000 a month with no stated overage. A store doing well on bundles has to ask what comes next rather than read it, and that is the wrong moment to be negotiating. Maturity is not the concern here: the app has been on the App Store since 15 September 2022 and carried 4.9 stars over 1,216 reviews on 4 September 2026 and 1,298 on 19 September, at the same average. The concern is where the money goes as you succeed. Two smaller things: the features most merchants picture when they think bundles are all paid: the guided single- and multi-step build-your-own-box builders sit on Essential at $29, and subscription bundles, add-ons and free gifts on Growth at $49 — none of them on the free plan, and the recent reviews that praise the app most warmly also praise the support team by name, which is a compliment to people rather than to a product that never needs them.

video:video.video:title: EcomXray Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The split between the two tiers is unusually clean, and worth seeing clearly: everything this app is described as doing, the margins, the net units, the restock advice, is free. The $29 buys editing, not insight. If you are happy making changes in the Shopify admin you already have, the free plan is the whole product and the paid one is a convenience layer over it.
The track record is the real caveat, and it has not moved. The app launched on 20 July 2026 and still had no reviews at all when we checked on 8 September, seven weeks later. Nothing is known about how it behaves at scale, how it handles a catalogue in the tens of thousands, or how quickly support answers, because nobody has said so in public.
And its numbers are only as good as your cost prices. Gross margin comes out of Shopify's own cost-per-item field, so if that field is empty or stale across your catalogue, the margin column is decoration. Fill the cost prices in first, then judge the app.

video:video.video:title: Essent Preorder Back in Stock Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The plans are cheap until a launch works. Each paid plan has a monthly allowance and then charges per use: on Lite, the 101st pre-order in a month costs $0.25, and so does every one after it, so a drop that sells 300 pre-orders on Lite costs $4.95 plus $50 in overage. Starter at $8.95 would have covered those 300 without any. Restock alerts are metered the same way, at $1.00 per 100 past the allowance. Pick the plan on the size of the launch you are planning, not on an average month, and check the usage screen while a campaign runs. The free plan's 25 pre-orders is enough to test the flow end to end, and the listing does not say what happens when a free store passes it.
Two features stores often assume are basic sit higher up. Mixed-cart validation, which stops a shopper from putting an in-stock item and a pre-order item in one order, starts on Starter at $8.95, as do campaigns limited to specific markets. A pre-order confirmation email sent from your own domain and scheduled campaigns start on Lite.
The critical reviews are few but specific. A South African store six months in wrote in September 2025 that the app counts inventory across every location, so a store with stock in a physical shop cannot run pre-orders for its online warehouse alone; the developer replied in October 2025 that the request had gone to its development team. An Australian store wrote in June 2026 that after turning the app off with stock back in, its code stayed behind and blocked the checkout button for days; the developer replied after an internal investigation. A US store in August 2025 reported unreliable email delivery and that the pre-order status did not appear on the customer's order confirmation. Earlier one-star reviews describe the app putting every product on pre-order instead of the chosen one, a discount lost when a shopper changed size or quantity, and an admin that would not load; the developer answered each by offering support.
The long list of positive reviews deserves

video:video.video:title: Essential Announcement Bar Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The bar the listing leads with is not on the free plan. The App Store copy opens on scrolling, marquee-style announcement bars, but the vendor's own help article on bar types says running-line announcements require a paid plan, and the pricing table puts them on Starter at $6.99. What the free plan does give you is a static bar and a rotating bar that cycles several messages; one merchant who installed it expecting the moving bar for free left a one-line complaint within half an hour. Scheduling, the feature that lets a flash-sale bar switch itself on and off, and the cart-page bar both start one step higher, on Essential at $9.99.
The view allowance is counted the expensive way. The help centre says a view is every render of a bar: each page load, each reload, and each bar when you run more than one on a page. A top bar sits on every page, so the free plan's 2,000 views is a few hundred browsing sessions a month on a small store, not 2,000 shoppers.
Running out does not cost money, it takes the bar down, and it stays down. Past the limit you get an email; three days later every published bar is unpublished, and the same article says that when views reset on the 1st the bars are not published again automatically. A store that misses the email loses its announcement for the rest of the month and then keeps missing it until someone notices and republishes.
The support that most reviews praise has one account on the other side. In April 2026 a UK merchant with twelve months on the app wrote that the team had published a page on her site without her consent and made styling changes that broke two sales pages shortly before a launch. Essential Apps replied that it was sorry and had only intended to help. If you give support access to fix a placement, say exactly what they may change. We have not installed the app.

video:video.video:title: Essential Countdown Timer Bar Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The free plan is smaller than it looks, because of what counts as a view. The help centre says a view is every time a timer loads: a shopper who refreshes the page, or browses three product pages with a timer on each, adds several views, and two timers on one page count twice. A thousand views a month is a few hundred browsing sessions on a store with a top bar on every page. Starter's 10,000 and Essential's 50,000 are counted the same way.
Running out does not cost money; it switches the timers off. There is no overage charge. When you reach the limit you get an email, and if you have not upgraded within three days every published timer is unpublished until views reset on the 1st of the month. The month you are most likely to hit the ceiling is the month of your biggest sale, so on a Black Friday campaign that is when the countdown disappears. If a promotion depends on the timer, size the plan on the traffic you expect at the peak rather than last month's, or watch the usage in the app while the campaign runs.
The cart timer, the one that tells shoppers their items are reserved, starts on the $9.99 Essential plan, not on Starter. Whether a claim like that is true depends on how you set it up, and the FTC treats false urgency and scarcity as deceptive practice; an evergreen fixed-minute timer starts fresh for each visitor, so keep it for offers that genuinely work that way. One incident is worth knowing about: a Chilean merchant with nearly three years on the app wrote that Shopify Support had traced a checkout button that redirected customers to an outside URL to a security vulnerability related to this app. Essential Apps replied that it fixed the issue within two hours of the first report, resolved the cause the same day and reported the incident to Shopify. We found no report of a repeat. We have not installed the app.

video:video.video:title: Essential Free Shipping Bar Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The cart page, where a free-shipping progress bar does most of its work, is not on the free plan and not on Starter either. Cart-page boosters start on Essential at $14.99 a month; Free and Starter cover the top bar and product pages. One merchant uninstalled within an hour over exactly that in February 2026, calling it the obvious place for the bar; the vendor replied that the limits are on the listing, which is true. Upsell products inside the bar and the revenue analytics the listing advertises are on the same $14.99 tier.
The app shows the goal; it does not give the free shipping. The help centre says the app does not touch your store settings, so you set the free-shipping rate yourself in Shopify's shipping settings, as a conditional rate based on order price, and you do it again for every market. If the threshold in the bar and the threshold in Shopify drift apart, the bar promises something checkout does not deliver. Currencies work the same way: a currency missing from the dropdown needs its own Shopify Market first.
Views are counted on every load of every widget, and the free plan's 1,000 a month is small for a bar that sits on every product page. The help centre says Preview mode and the theme customiser are not counted; one merchant wrote in March 2026 that editing product pages in the customiser used up views, so check the counter after a design session. Past the limit there is no charge, but three days after the warning email the banners are unpublished until the 1st.
Two older complaints are worth knowing. A merchant in Japan wrote that the bar did not update when a shopper switched variants and prices; the vendor answered that real-time variant updates are supported and offered to help. And a UK merchant wrote in 2023 that uninstalling left code behind in the theme. Check the theme after removal. We have not installed the app.

video:video.video:title: Essential Loyalty Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Two things to read closely before you pay. The meter is honest — loyalty-influenced orders, not all orders — and that is genuinely in your favour, but it also means you cannot work out your tier from your order count. A store doing 3,000 orders a month with little repeat business may sit on Free; one doing 800 with a loyal base may not. Measure your repeat and referral orders for a month before you choose.
The second is an oddity on the listing itself. The free plan advertises an 'Advanced loyalty point program' while Starter at $10 advertises a 'Free loyalty point program', which read literally means the paid tier offers less on that line. It is almost certainly a labelling slip rather than a real downgrade, but it is the kind of line worth confirming with support before you upgrade for it.

video:video.video:title: Essential Trust Badges Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The free plan is generous on views and tight on badges. It allows 5,000 views a month, more than the vendor's countdown and announcement-bar apps give away, but only one product-page banner or one block of three icons, plus payment icons. A store that wants a shipping promise under the add-to-cart button and a separate guarantee block further down is already on Starter, and uploading your own icon instead of choosing from the library also starts there.
The badge people most often want, the one next to the checkout button, is on the $9.99 Essential plan. The help centre says cart-page and cart-drawer badges are not available on Free or Starter, and adds two limits that are easy to miss: the app supports your theme's own cart drawer only, not third-party cart-drawer apps, and a badge placed with the custom-position method appears on the cart page but no longer inside the drawer. If your store uses a slide-cart app, check this before you pay for the plan that unlocks it.
Views are counted per widget load, so every badge on a page adds a view each time the page opens, including your own visits; preview mode and the theme customiser are not counted. Past the limit nothing is charged, but three days after the warning email the badges are unpublished until the 1st of the month. The critical reviews are few, three one-star and two three-star out of 1,163, and they are about setup rather than billing: one store gave up after a week trying to show two product-page banners, which the vendor replied needed two product-page badges rather than one product and one cart badge, and one wanted more design options without writing CSS. A badge is also a claim: show only guarantees, returns and security marks you actually offer. We have not installed the app.

video:video.video:title: Essential Upsell & Cross Sell Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The plans are metered on revenue the app says it generated, and the free plan's $100 a month is a small allowance. A store whose upsells work moves up the ladder because they work: $500 on Starter, $1,000 on Essential, and only Professional at $39.99 a month has no limit. Neither the listing nor the vendor's page explains how that revenue is attributed to the app or what happens when a store passes its limit, so ask support before you rely on the free plan in a busy month. The ceiling is the reassuring part: the bill cannot go above $39.99 a month, however much the offers sell.
The two pricing pages do not agree on the cart. On the Shopify listing, cart-page offers start on Essential at $19.99; the vendor's own page lists them on Starter at $9.99 too. The cart drawer is where many stores want an upsell, so confirm in the app which plan unlocks it before you pick Starter.
The free plan is a real plan, but it does not look like one at install. A US merchant wrote in February 2026 that the app advertised a free plan and then pushed a free trial; the vendor replied that the free plan has a revenue limit and needs a Shopify approval step. Read the approval screen rather than closing it.
The app asks for a lot of data. The listing says it needs to view and edit customers, products, orders, discounts and the online store. Two US merchants dropped it to one star in 2024 and 2025 over permissions that covered customers' personal details and recent orders; the vendor answered that the access is for the performance analytics merchants asked for. If you keep a tight data policy, read the permission screen before you approve it.
The rest of the criticism is about fit with a theme or a store setup. A French merchant uninstalled in November 2025 because widgets did not show on pages whose product handle had been translated; the vendor replied in February 2026 that product targeting now uses the product ID instead of the handle. A UK merchant wrote in September 2025 that it did

video:video.video:title: Evey Events Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Nobody gets caught by the monthly fee here; they get caught by the per-ticket one. On Lite the app is free to install and then takes a dollar off every ticket you sell, which is invisible until you sell volume and then is the largest line on the invoice. Work out your monthly ticket count before you install anything, because that single number picks your plan: under 76 stay on Lite, 76 to 120 move to Growth, 120 to 560 move to Standard, above that Professional. Getting this wrong is not a small error -- at 300 tickets a month the gap between the best and worst choice is about $65 every month.

video:video.video:title: Expandi Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: There is no free tier and no cheap entry — Expandi starts at $99 a month per seat, and the friendlier $79 assumes annual commitment. It's also LinkedIn automation, which sits in a grey zone against LinkedIn's own terms: powerful for outreach, but a platform-risk you own.

video:video.video:title: ExpertSender Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The $450/mo floor and the 30k-monthly-visits target make this an established-store tool, not a starter one: below that traffic the platform can't pay for itself, and there is no self-serve plan to test it cheaply first.

video:video.video:title: FBtrack Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
A pixel app earns its fee by being dull: it has to fire every event, every day, and you only notice it when it stops. The critical reviews on FBtrack's listing are about the day it stopped. In June 2026 a Spanish merchant with twelve months on the app wrote that tracking had stopped from one day to the next without warning; Shark Byte apologised and replied that the outage was caused by an incident. In December 2024 an Indian store two years in reported that Add to Cart events had not arrived since it started using the app and that a support ticket had gone unanswered; the developer apologised for the missing event and the slow reply. In April 2023 a merchant said only the Purchase event failed to reach Facebook on one store, which support then fixed. With 22 reviews in eight years there is not much else to weigh these against.
Much of the basic job is available for nothing. Meta's own Facebook & Instagram app for Shopify is free to install and sets up a conversion pixel, and the three apps the App Store lists next to FBtrack for the same job are free, free to install or have a free plan. What FBtrack adds is several pixels at once, such as a pixel per collection or a backup pixel, and TikTok, Snapchat and Pinterest tags from the same screen. If you run one Meta pixel, check what the free route already gives you before you pay $10 a month.
There is no product website. The domain in the support address, fbtrack.app, has no site behind it, and the app runs from optiapps.xyz, where the only page is a login screen. The listing's feature tags include campaign management and bid optimization, but the plans describe pixels, the Conversions API and server-side events only: FBtrack sends data to your ad platforms and does not run your ads. A 2024 review from Italy said charges continued two months after the merchant uninstalled and cancelled; the developer apologised. Check your next Shopify bill after you remove it. We have not installed the app.

video:video.video:title: Fast Bundle Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The most important thing about this app is not on its App Store listing. On 17 July 2026 Fast Bundle detected what its own status page calls a security attack; Shopify removed the app from the App Store as a precaution and deactivated it on existing stores, so merchants found it simply gone. It was restored to limited visibility on 30 July and fully searchable again on 3 August, after Shopify reviewed an incident report and a third-party vulnerability and penetration test. The vendor states its investigation and testing found no indication that any customer, store or shopper data was accessed, exposed or leaked, and that 2,405 stores had reinstalled by early August. Shopify's own words, quoted on that page, are that the app “has been restored to limited visibility”.
Nobody outside the process can verify what was reached, and neither the vendor nor Shopify has published the technical detail. What is verifiable is the shape of the disruption: a storefront-facing app pulled without warning, deactivated on live stores, and roughly two weeks coming back. If your bundles carry your average order value, that is the risk you are underwriting — not because it is likely to recur, but because it has happened once and the app sits in the path to checkout.
The review record needs reading with that date in mind. 5.0 from 3,031 reviews is exceptional, and the breakdown is 3,000 at five stars against 19 at one. But most of that history predates July 2026, and Shopify app ratings skew high because merchants are prompted for them. What an average cannot tell you is how a vendor handles an incident, and on that the status page is the better evidence: dated, specific, quoting Shopify directly, and correcting its own earlier estimates in public. That is a good sign about communication rather than about security.
One practical hazard came out of the outage and has not gone away. While the app was delisted, other apps renamed themselves to include “Fast Bundle” — the vendor names Fast

video:video.video:title: Feedvisor Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest structure: Feedvisor publishes no price, so the quote you are given is the only figure that counts — amounts circulating online come from third parties, not from Feedvisor. What it is famous for (the algorithmic Buy-Box strategy that holds prices UP, ad management, analysts) sits on the higher tiers of its own plan comparison: this is enterprise software for serious catalogs. If your Amazon revenue can’t absorb an enterprise quote as a small percentage, simpler repricers are the rational choice.

video:video.video:title: Feedyio Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two gates decide your bill and neither is about how much value the feeds create. The first is catalogue size: the ladder counts products and variants, and it runs further than the Shopify listing suggests — the listing stops at Pro ($29.99, 6,000 products) and says additional plans are available, while the vendor's own pricing page publishes five more tiers up to $119.99 for 65,000 products. The second is freshness: the free tier updates products once a day and hourly updates start at $9.99, which matters when stock moves faster than a day. Multi-market and multi-language feeds only appear at $19.99. The app is also younger and smaller than the shelf leaders: launched 16 May 2022 by happyapps.cz in Prague, with 115 reviews against thousands for the established Google Shopping feed apps. And the standout integrations — Heureka, Zboží.cz, Árukereső, Glami, Favi, Kaufland — are Central and Eastern European channels; that is the app's real edge, but it is not an edge if you only sell through Google and Meta.

video:video.video:title: Flocksy Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: 'Unlimited' means unlimited queue, not unlimited throughput: work happens at your plan's daily capacity, so a big launch week still needs planning, and turnaround expectations are where subscription-design relationships sour. The economics are simple and honest — against even one freelance designer's day rate, the math works IF you feed it steady volume; if your design needs are sporadic, a flat monthly fee is paying for silence — unused hours do bank, but only for 30 days.

video:video.video:title: Frase Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The article quotas pinch if you publish at volume (overage docs bill each), and it's a research-and-optimization tool, not a magic ranking button — it speeds up briefs, it doesn't replace the writing or the backlinks. In our test on 20 October 2026 the writer put back a claim we had rejected, now credited to the National Institutes of Health, and ignored our audience and 'no product tips' instructions, so every generated article needs a human check on its claims.

video:video.video:title: FullEnrich Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pay-on-success model is refreshingly honest, but note the 10x: phone numbers eat credits ten times faster than emails, so a calling-heavy motion consumes budget quickly — model your email/phone mix. As a waterfall over 20+ providers, its hit rate genuinely beats single databases; the flip side is you're paying a premium per contact versus querying one source that might have sufficed.

video:video.video:title: Gelato Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free plan is genuinely usable, so the honest question is only whether Gelato+ earns its fee — and that depends entirely on volume: below ~10 orders a month the discounts won't cover the subscription. Its real edge is local production in 30+ countries (fast, cheaper international shipping), but that means quality and product availability can vary slightly by region and print partner. Sample your key products before scaling.

video:video.video:title: GeoStock Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Know what this is before you buy it: despite the name it is a storefront widget, not an inventory system. It displays the stock you already track in Shopify per location, and adds a store-locator map — it does not manage, forecast or reconcile anything. If you came looking for multi-location inventory management, that is a different category and a different budget. What it does do well is close a specific gap: a shopper who can see that a nearby store has the item is a shopper who does not abandon.

video:video.video:title: Geotargetly Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The meter is pageviews, not visitors, and each product consumes its own pageview on the same page visit — so a redirect plus a popup bills twice. Run out and you get two days to upgrade or re-subscribe before services stop. The friendlier advertised numbers are the yearly rates; month-to-month runs about 25% higher. And the dependency worth pricing in: the rules run from a script you drop into your site, so they exist only while that script is served. Stop the subscription and every visitor sees the same page again, wherever they are.

video:video.video:title: GrapeLeads Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: You are billed per result, not per usable lead: one credit opens the search and one more is charged for every business it returns, so a broad filter burns credits whether or not the results are worth calling. The packs are small enough that this is cheap to test ($28 for 50 credits) but it is the wrong shape if you want volume prospecting at a predictable monthly cost — there is no subscription at all. The site also still 404s its own /pricing link while the real list sits at /buy-credits/, which is an odd look for a tool sold to web professionals. And the niche (Google-Maps businesses without websites) is the real product: judge the data on one pack before you go further.

video:video.video:title: Grapevine Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The flat price is the whole pricing page, which cuts both ways. There is no free tier and no small plan, so from day fifteen the app costs $25 a month whether it collects four responses or forty thousand — a low-volume store pays the same as a high-volume one, and several of the nearest alternatives do publish a free plan. The second thing to weigh is access rather than price: the listing's data section asks for customer data including sensitive, device and activity data, plus orders, staff accounts and the online store, which is a lot of reach for a survey tool and worth reading the privacy policy over. The evidence base is otherwise good for a Shopify app — launched 17 August 2017 by Union Works Apps in London, and 232 reviews on 13 October 2026 of which 225 are five-star and none below four.

video:video.video:title: Gushwork Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
One published number, and it is the floor. $900 a month is where Gushwork starts and the pricing page never says where it stops — the FAQ puts the final figure down to page volume, growth speed and paid support, confirmed on a call. The honest reading of that page is therefore not “this costs $900” but “this costs at least $900, and you find out the rest on the phone.” That is a planning problem for exactly the small business it targets, and it is avoidable: the two nearest AI-SEO products we carry both publish their whole ladder, BabyLoveGrowth at €99 and €399 a month and Alli AI at $299 and $599, so you can size those against a budget before you speak to anyone.
The second thing is that you are buying a service more than a seat. There is no free plan, no trial and no self-serve sign-up; the only route in is Book a Demo, onboarding is put at “less than 30 days”, and Gushwork does the research, writing, publishing and optimisation. That is the appeal if you have no marketer. It is also a dependency, and the pages it publishes live on your site.
Third — and to their credit they say this themselves — it is slow. The FAQ puts first qualified leads at “month 3 to 4” and adds, “We won’t promise leads in week one.” At $900 a month that is roughly $2,700 to $3,600 spent before the thing you bought is expected to show up. Budget for the wait rather than the first invoice.
And check the fit before the price, because Gushwork’s own qualifier is stricter than its marketing. Its sign-up form says the platform “works best for sales led B2B businesses” — quote requests, consultation calls, service inquiries — and tells anyone whose customers can buy or sign up directly on the site that they are “not the right fit (yet)”.
