video:video.video:title: Hello Bar Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The meter is views, not results: every visitor who sees a popup counts against your quota, so a traffic spike eats the allowance regardless of how many emails you actually captured, and at the limit the campaigns pause until the next billing cycle — a busy site outgrows the entry tier fast. And the honest fundamental of every popup tool: it amplifies an offer, it doesn't create one. A weak lead magnet with a beautiful popup is still a weak lead magnet, and aggressive full-screen takeovers can cost more goodwill (and Core Web Vitals) than they capture.

video:video.video:title: HubSpot Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Three numbers on this pricing page are not what they look like, and they compound.
The first is the $7. It is the number in large black type on the Starter card, and the $20 beside it in small grey type is the list price. The banner above the table explains why: up to 65% off Starter, new customers only, for a limited time. So $7 is an introductory rate and $20 is what the seat costs afterwards — a 186% step for a system that by then holds your contact database, which is the single most painful kind of software to leave.
The second is the $800. Professional carries a required one-time onboarding fee of $3,000, disclosed in a footnote under the card rather than in the price. Year one on Professional is therefore $800 × 12 + $3,000 = $12,600 if you pay annually, or $890 × 12 + $3,000 = $13,680 month to month. The onboarding adds roughly a third to the first year, and no amount of shopping around removes it — it is mandatory. Enterprise does the same thing at $7,000 on top of $43,200 a year.
The third is the seat count, because it is not the meter that usually bites. Professional includes 3 Core Seats and 2,000 marketing contacts. For a marketing platform, contacts are the axis that grows on its own: your list gets bigger whether or not you hire anyone, and the contact tier moves the bill without anyone deciding to upgrade. Price your next two years on the list you expect to have, not the team you have now.
One more thing worth knowing before you start on Free. The free tier is genuinely usable — two users, 1,000 contacts, no expiry — and that is exactly how the ladder is designed to work. The step from Starter to Professional is not incremental: at list prices a three-seat team goes from $60 a month to $890 plus $3,000 once, which is roughly fifteen times the monthly cost. Whatever you build on Free, build it knowing where the next rung is.

video:video.video:title: Iconosquare Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Its depth is strongest on Instagram and the core networks; if your priority platform sits outside its best-supported set, coverage thins. Analytics is where it shines — scheduling and community features exist but aren't always as deep as dedicated publishers. And the per-seat, per-profile tiering means agencies managing many brands climb toward the Custom plan quicker than the headline Starter price suggests: Starter and Launch carry one seat and five profiles at most, Scale three seats and up to 20 profiles at €219 billed yearly, and only Custom goes beyond that.

video:video.video:title: InboxAlly Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: This is a premium, seed-list-based deliverability tool, and the price reflects it — Starter alone is well above casual warm-up apps, so it only makes sense if inbox placement is genuinely costing you real revenue. It improves sender reputation through engagement signals, but it's not a magic fix for bad content or a purchased list: deliverability still depends on how you actually send. Buy it when the math (lost revenue from spam-foldering) clearly beats the monthly fee.

video:video.video:title: Influencer Hero Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The three-month minimum is the real commitment, and there is no free trial to soften it. Every plan carries it, so the smallest honest entry price is not $519 but three months — $1,557 on the quarterly rate, $1,947 if you pay monthly. An influencer programme takes longer than four weeks to show you anything, so the vendor is not being unreasonable; it just means the decision is a quarter of spending rather than a month of trying.
Read which column you are quoted. The public pricing page leads with the quarterly rate, so $519 is what gets repeated — but billed monthly the same plan is $649, a quarter more. Pro is $839 or $1,049, Business $1,992 or $2,490. The 20% and 30% savings are genuine and check out exactly against the monthly rate; the trap is only that the advertised number already has the discount in it.
What the ladder actually meters is worth understanding, because it is better than it looks. A reach-out counts once, at the moment you first contact a new influencer. Every follow-up, reply and ongoing conversation with that same creator after that is unlimited and never draws the quota down again — so the meter counts new relationships opened, not messages sent. Standard's 1,000 a month is therefore 1,000 new creators, which is a great many, and nurturing the ones who answer costs nothing.
Hitting the cap gives you two routes and the vendor recommends one of them against its own short-term interest: buy a top-up, or move up a tier. Their own documentation says brands who top up once tend to keep doing it, so repeated top-ups erode the saving from staying low. No top-up rate is published anywhere, which is the one number still missing from an otherwise unusually open account.
Payouts are capped per plan, and the cap is what pushes paying brands up the ladder: 20 a month on Standard, 200 on Pro, 500 on Business and unlimited only on Enterprise. The Business card briefly said unlimited after a site revamp; the vendor corrected it, and on 24 September 2026 t

video:video.video:title: Instapage Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's premium-priced and only justified by serious ad spend — Create is $79 a month billed annually for 15,000 unique monthly visitors, and the price per thousand barely improves as you climb, so the higher tiers buy features rather than cheaper traffic. The 14-day trial needs a card and carries its own cap of 2,500 visitors; crossing it ends the trial and starts the paid plan by itself. And there's the ownership question the feature list does not raise: publishing to your own domain means pointing a CNAME at Instapage — their help centre carries a per-registrar guide for exactly that — so the page is served by them and lives as long as the subscription does. Their own docs add a second catch worth knowing before you standardise on it: “we lock domains under the first Instapage account that uses them”. Treat these pages as rented campaign infrastructure, not as part of your site, and keep the copy somewhere you control.

video:video.video:title: Intelis Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The ladder counts variants, not products, and that is where stores get caught. A catalogue of forty garments in five sizes and three colours is six hundred variants, so a shop most people would call small lands on the $179 tier rather than the $49 one. Count your variants, not your line items, before you read the price.
The vendor's own numbers above Premium used to contradict each other, and that is worth knowing mainly because it has been fixed. On 21 August 2026 the Shopify listing said Business was $399 while intelis.ai/pricing said $499 with a $4,990 annual rate, and the homepage and the pricing page gave Enterprise as $749 and $849. Re-read on 8 September 2026, all three pages agree: Business $399 ($3,990 a year), Enterprise $749 ($7,490) for up to 10,000 SKUs. If you are working from a comparison written earlier this year, check its figures against the listing.
And automatic repricing is not a switch you leave alone. The matching is AI-driven across Google Shopping and competitor sites, and a mismatched listing quietly reprices the wrong product, while an unbounded rule set on a busy category is how a store races itself to the bottom. Set floor prices before you turn dynamic pricing on, and audit what the automatch decided in the first fortnight.

video:video.video:title: Kartra Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: If your core need is polished course delivery, Kajabi's creator features are stronger; Kartra wins on all-in-one breadth, not course depth.

video:video.video:title: Kedra Checkout Rules & Upsells Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free plan runs a single rule with a single condition, and Starter only three, and the listing and Kedra's own documentation disagree on whether that limit is per rule type or in total. The app cannot add anything visual to the checkout page, and rules skip draft orders made in the Shopify admin. We found no published refund or cancellation policy.

video:video.video:title: Kit Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Three honest notes. Subscriber-based pricing counts everyone on your list — cold subscribers cost the same as fans, so prune before you price. The free plan changed shape in 2026: it now runs to 10,000 subscribers rather than 1,000 (re-verified 2026-09-02), but Visual Automations and email sequences came out of it, so the free tier sends and captures without automating anything — what puts you on Creator at $39/mo, or $33/mo paid yearly, is wanting a welcome sequence rather than list growth. And the 35% price hike in 2025 changed the value math: the free tier is still arguably the best in creator email, but paid tiers now deserve comparison shopping rather than default loyalty. The creator-first features (tip jars, paid newsletters, recommendations) remain the real differentiator.

video:video.video:title: Kite Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: 'Free to install' is doing a lot of work on this listing. The free plan covers the first 50 discount orders a month, and the same panel says $29 a month is billed once you pass them — so it is a threshold with an invoice behind it, not a free tier you can settle on. A store running one decent promotion will cross 50 discounted orders in days and be on Starter money without choosing to upgrade. The second catch is written on the plans themselves: Free and Starter are both labelled 'Not for Shopify Advanced and Plus', so if you are on either of those Shopify plans your real entry price is the $49 Growth tier, not the $29 the listing leads with. And the feature most likely to sell the app to a large merchant — free gifts added at checkout — is marked Plus only and sits in the $99 Pro tier, which means the Plus stores it is built for pay $1,188 a year to reach it.

video:video.video:title: Kiwi Sizing Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free plan is not limited by the chart count most people assume. Three charts is generous for a small catalogue; the real limit is the Kiwi watermark sitting on your storefront, and removing it is what the $7.99 buys. Judge the free tier on whether you can live with that watermark in front of customers, not on how many charts you get. And read the small print above Plus and Ultimate before you upgrade: both add order-volume charges that the App Store listing never quantifies, while Premium says in writing that it has none.

video:video.video:title: Koala Bundles Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The meter is revenue, and it counts more of it than you might expect. The help centre defines bundle offer revenue as the whole value of the bundle a customer buys through a Koala offer, not the uplift over the normal price: a $70 three-pack adds $70 to the counter even if one unit on its own would have sold for $30. Kickstart's $1,000 a month is therefore roughly fourteen of those $70 bundles, and a store selling a few bundles a day is past it in the first week. Scale Koala's $5,000 is the realistic starting point for a store that actually uses bundles as a main offer, and above that the next step is Unlimited at $59.99, three times the price.
What happens at the ceiling matters more than the price. There is no overage charge; instead the store owner gets an email at 80% and at 100%, and if nobody upgrades within 24 hours the offers are paused until the first of the next month. A 24-hour window is short: a cap reached on a Friday night during a promotion can take the bundles off the product pages before anyone reads the email. If bundles are part of a campaign, set the plan on the revenue you expect at the peak, and check the usage counter in the app while it runs.
The counter is only as good as the attribution behind it. On 29 September 2026 a US merchant with four months on the app wrote that Koala counted an order as a bundle sale when the customer bought one unit of a buy-three offer plus other items and never received the discount. We could not check that claim, but it is worth testing on your own store, because on this pricing model an overcount is not just a flattering report: it moves you towards the cap. Other critical reviews describe a bundle that could not map each variant to its own SKU for the supplier (July 2025), products shown as sold out despite stock (December 2025), and a widget that loaded slowly; the help centre says a delay of four to five seconds goes away once you add the app block to the product template instead of relying on the embed.

video:video.video:title: Koala Gifts Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The price follows your Shopify plan, not how much you use the app. A store on Shopify Advanced pays $49.99 a month for the same feature list a Basic store gets for $9.99, even if it runs one gift offer a quarter. The fee does not move by itself: the help centre says that if you upgrade your Shopify plan you have 14 days to upgrade in the app as well to keep your offers active. Downgrades are pro-rated; cancellations are not.
The gift mechanics have a few traps that the help centre documents itself. The gift product must carry a normal price above zero, because the app gives it away with a 100% discount; a gift priced at zero and published to the storefront can be bought without any of the offer's conditions. A gift can also flip from free to full price at checkout when the customer adds another discount code, unless that other discount is set to combine with product discounts. And a minimum-spend rule reads the price before discounts: with a $100 threshold, a $150 product with a 50% code still earns the gift at $75. The vendor's workaround is to use compare-at prices instead of discount codes.
There is a ceiling on offers, set by Shopify rather than by the plan. Shopify allows 25 automatic discounts per store, and the app packs about ten offers into each, which the help centre puts at roughly 90 to 250 offers. Disabling one Koala discount in Shopify's own discount screen can switch off several offers at once.
The critical reviews are few but specific. A US merchant wrote in March 2025, after six days, that the gift was not applied to orders correctly and that they had to refund customers. An Australian merchant disliked the long generated discount code the gift shows at checkout (February 2025). A US merchant who paid $599 a year for another ProfitKoala app objected in November 2025 to needing a separate subscription for BOGO offers, and a merchant in Ecuador noted in April 2025 that the app had been free and now costs money. video:video.video:title: Koongo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The headline price is a base, not a bill. Each paid plan includes 1,000 items, 5 feeds, one marketplace wizard and 100 orders a month, and the listing says plainly that surcharges apply for extras used across all four of those dimensions. For a store with a real catalogue selling on several European marketplaces, every one of those limits is one you pass in week one. Price your own numbers on koongo.com's surcharge table before you take $39 seriously.
The two pricing pages also do not quote the same bill. The App Store lists $39, $79 and $119 and bills in USD. koongo.com lists €35, €69 and €99 and states that all prices exclude VAT. Depending on where you trade and how you are registered, those are meaningfully different amounts for the same plan, and nothing on either page reconciles them.
Then the record, which is the most useful thing on this listing. 4.4 from 98 reviews is the lowest average in this category among the apps Shopify shows beside it, and the breakdown explains why: 84 five-star ratings sit alongside six one-star ones. The critical reviews are specific rather than vague, which makes them worth reading in full. In July 2026 a Belgian merchant described a repricer set to Monitoring Mode that still blocked updates to live Bol offers because of MinimumPrice errors, so a delivery-promise change never reached the marketplace. In January 2026 a UK merchant described unresolved integration errors on OnBuy and a refused refund, with Koongo replying publicly that they had reached out several times without response. Neither is disqualifying on its own. Together they describe an app whose complexity is real and whose marketplace integrations sometimes need support to untangle — which is consistent with the vendor's own listing offering personal onboarding for complex setups.
One more line to read before you install: the listing states the app views sensitive customer data as well as device and activity data, and can view and edit products, orders and custom

video:video.video:title: Kumo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Five stars over nine reviews is not a track record, and the age makes that worse rather than better. The app launched on 21 November 2024, so it has had close to two years on the App Store to collect them. Nine reviews in that window is a small installed base, and a small installed base is what decides whether an app is still maintained in 2028 — the rating tells you the nine are happy, not that the app is safe to build a wholesale channel on.
The second plan is a trap for anyone who reads the ladder as a feature ladder. PLUS costs twice B2B and the three things it adds — company registration, catalog assignment, checkout integration — are all labelled Shopify Plus on the listing itself. On a standard Shopify plan the extra $15 a month buys nothing you can switch on.

video:video.video:title: Landingi Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: You trade away the high-end optimisation: no AI traffic routing like Unbounce's Smart Traffic, no real-time collaboration, and thinner technical control (script containers). Excellent value, but not the conversion-optimisation powerhouse.

video:video.video:title: LangShop Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two things sit awkwardly next to each other in the plan table. The headline promise is 'unlimited words', but every tier caps how many products you may translate and how many languages you may run, so the meter you actually pay is catalogue size. The named engines — OpenAI, DeepL Pro, Google Cloud Translation — now start on Basic at $10 a month (they were a $40 Standard feature when we read the page in September 2026), but dynamic content, metaobjects, third-party app strings and export of your translations still start at Standard. The Shopify listing also understates the ladder: it stops at Advanced and links to 'more pricing plans', while the vendor's pricing page publishes Pro at $120, Enterprise at $250 and Unlimited at $500 — and API access, which no listing tier mentions, starts at Pro. The app is old enough to judge (launched 15 September 2016, developer Aheadworks) and most of its 473 reviews are positive (13 October 2026), but 24 of them are one-star, and the recent negative ones are specific rather than vague: a Slovak store reporting that metafield translations ignore both the AI store context and the glossary rules, and a Swedish store of almost three years reporting that products duplicated from another product carry the wrong translation across. If metafields or duplicated products are central to your catalogue, test exactly that during the trial.

video:video.video:title: Later Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The Starter caps are where the price really lives: 30 posts per profile and 3 months of analytics run out fast for an active brand, pushing real users toward Growth — so compare at the tier you'll actually need, not the entry price. Later's visual-first planning (born from Instagram) is still its strength; if your world is link-in-bio commerce and grids, that focus earns its seat.

video:video.video:title: Leadfeeder Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The words doing the work are 'starting at'. What actually sets your price is how many companies you identify a month, and the tier table sits behind a 'How is the price calculated?' link rather than on the plan cards, which still read 'Tiered'. Opened, it shows that €79 buys up to 50 identified companies a month on Discover; 51-100 is €109, 101-200 €139, 201-400 €179, 401-500 €249 and 501-1,000 €309, all billed annually (pricing page, read 12 October 2026). Month to month costs 43% more on the same tier (€113 against €79, €441 against €309), and Scale is annual-only, so the tier most growing teams land on cannot be tried for a month.

video:video.video:title: Leadpages Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's the value pick, not the optimisation pick — if you're spending big on ads, Unbounce's Smart Traffic and Instapage's 1:1 personalisation go deeper.

video:video.video:title: LearnWorlds Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The detail most people miss is Starter's $5-per-paid-enrollment fee — at any real sales volume it quietly makes Starter more expensive than the flat Pro Trainer plan, so the "cheap" tier often isn't. Starter also runs on a single admin seat and 24/5 email support against 24/7 above it, and the branded mobile app is a separate add-on whose price the pricing page no longer states. Price it against your expected enrollment volume, not the sticker.

video:video.video:title: LettrLabs Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Direct mail only pays off with a tight list and a real offer — it's a leverage channel, not a cheap thing to test blindly.

video:video.video:title: LifterLMS Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Taking payments needs a paid bundle, and every bundle renews at twice the first-year price: Earth $398, Universe $598 and Infinity $1,598 a year. LifterLMS is a WordPress plugin, so hosting, updates, backups and theme compatibility are yours to manage. Earth covers one site and one support user. We have not used LifterLMS ourselves.

video:video.video:title: Livestorm Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: This is a bet on attendance that you place a year in advance. You buy credits up front — €2.50 each in euros, $3.00 in dollars, set separately rather than converted — and a credit is spent per unique participant per session, so a four-part series to the same 200 people is 800 credits, not 200, which is €2,000. A webinar that does better than expected runs you out, and the page is now clear about what that means: new attendees cannot join until you buy a higher tier. The page publishes the per-attendee rate but never a total. Before you commit, count sessions times expected attendees for the whole year, and plan to use them within the billing year, because Livestorm's help centre (read 22 October 2026) says unused credits do not roll over. There is no pause option either, and cancelling after the renewal date brings no refund.

video:video.video:title: Loyalino Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Reach your plan's order limit and the program does not cost more, it stops. Their FAQ is explicit about it: at a finite plan limit the loyalty program pauses until the next calendar month or an eligible upgrade, and there are no per-order overage fees. For most metered apps that would be a mercy. For a loyalty program it means points quietly stop accruing for your customers partway through your busiest month, which is exactly when you least want it, and the free plan's ceiling of 200 orders is reached by a store doing seven orders a day. The ladder pushes the same direction: on their published rates the price per loyalty order gets worse with every step up rather than better - about $0.058 an order at Starter's 500, $0.065 at Essential's 2,000 and $0.071 at Growth's 7,000, which is our arithmetic on their figures at each plan's ceiling. And the thing they sell hardest is the thing you cannot check from outside: one-to-one support on every plan including the free one, and custom development included on the paid ones, from the people who wrote the code. That is a real differentiator if it holds. The app launched on 16 June 2026 and carries no reviews at all, so nothing independent stands behind it yet.

video:video.video:title: Lusha Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: A phone number costs 5 credits, so the credit counts on the plan cards buy far fewer phone numbers than contacts. Annual credits are granted upfront and reset at the end of the year, and plans renew automatically unless you cancel at least 14 days before the renewal date. Seats are capped per plan (1 on Starter, 2 on Pro, 5 on Premium). Lusha's data partly comes from a community programme in which members share contact details from their email headers and signatures, which matters if you sell into privacy-sensitive markets. We have not used Lusha ourselves.

video:video.video:title: Nextify.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The plans are sold in videos and images; the meter runs in credits per second, and the two do not reconcile. Every tier's headline count works out at 20 credits a video and 2 credits an image — 1,000 credits become “up to 50 videos” and “up to 500 images”, 3,000 become 150 and 1,500, 8,000 become 400 and 4,000. The app's own credit table prices video per second of output: Seedance 2.0, the model the editor pre-selects, is 12 credits a second at 720p, so the default four-second clip costs 48. We generated one and watched the balance fall from 3,000 to 2,952. That makes Pro 62 clips a month rather than 150, and 16 if you use the 15-second maximum. The 20-credit figure is reachable, but only on the 5-credit-a-second model at four seconds. The image claim has no such escape hatch: the cheapest image model in the table is 7 credits and the pre-selected one is 10, so nothing in the product costs the 2 credits those counts assume, and Starter's 500 images is nearer 100.

video:video.video:title: NiceJob Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Reporting and customization are fairly basic, and the Sites website add-on carries a $199 setup fee on top of its $99 a month. It automates review collection genuinely well, but if you want deep analytics or granular control over timing and wording, it can feel restrictive. And the honest fundamental: automation only amplifies the service you actually deliver. It keeps the review stream fresh and steady (which matters — stale reviews lose trust fast, and AI search increasingly recommends businesses on review signals), but it cannot manufacture a reputation you haven't earned.

video:video.video:title: Nutshell Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Full API access is included on every plan, so integrations are not the cost trap here — the add-ons are. Marketing at $49/mo and Engagement at $16/user/mo sit on top of the seat price, and email and SMS are billed by contact count and message volume, so the marketing side can outgrow the CRM itself. SSO and SQL data access are Enterprise-only.

video:video.video:title: Omneky Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pricing page gives credits per month (200, 1,000 or 4,000) but not what an image or video costs in credits, so you cannot tell from it how many ads a plan produces. Lite allows one brand, one seat and one connected ad channel, and avatar and clone videos start on Standard at $99 a month. We have not used Omneky ourselves.

video:video.video:title: PagePulse Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The ladder is metered on tracked pages, not people: Starter buys two pages, and every card below Scale lists unlimited collaborators, although the FAQ says workspace members are what you pay for. The $29 to $199 headline prices are annual-billing rates; month to month the paid tiers cost $36 to $249. AI insights are capped per month per tier, and 'Traffic included' carries a fair-use asterisk. If you run a whole content site, count your pages before you count on the price.

video:video.video:title: Parallel AI Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free tier is genuinely free -- 50 credits a month, no card -- and it is the only way to answer the question the pricing page leaves open. Data credits are priced per unit, but platform credits are not: nowhere does the page say what a content run, an agent conversation or an outreach step costs, and those are the actions the plan is sold on. So spend those 50 credits on the workflow you would actually buy this for and read Usage & Billing, which tracks consumption by feature, model and timestamp. Until you have that number, 2,000 credits a month is a quantity without a unit.

video:video.video:title: PartnerStack Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The reporting counts clicks and calls them customers. A record in the Partner API's customers endpoint is a tracked click, not a signup: on 29 July 2026 a single bare curl against one tracking link at 07:09:01 UTC produced a customer record at 07:09:02, with no browser, no account and has_paid false. Read that endpoint's length as signups and you will report volume that never existed. The second half of the problem is that there is no referring-URL field anywhere in the partnership data, so you can see that a link was clicked and never learn which of your pages earned it — which is exactly the thing you need to decide what to write next.

video:video.video:title: Pickeasy Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The rate features depend on something Pickeasy does not sell. Charging your own delivery or shipping rates through the app needs Shopify's Carrier Calculated Shipping API, and Shopify, not Logbase, decides whether your plan includes it. The vendor says so itself in a public reply from November 2025: the API is needed only for rates set inside Pickeasy, and the rest of the app works without it. That still covers a large part of the ladder, from rates by price and weight on Starter to multi-condition and day-of-week rates on Premium. Reviewers from January 2024, June 2025 and August 2025 say they set the app up before finding that their Shopify plan did not include the API, and one wrote that getting it would have meant at least $100 a month more to Shopify on top of the app's own fee. Check your plan for carrier-calculated shipping before you build rates.
The free plan counts your whole store. Its limit is 10 orders a month, and the vendor's pricing page says that means total store orders, not orders that book a pickup or delivery slot. A live store that sells at all is on Starter within days, so treat $9.99 as the entry price and the free tier as a way to build the setup on a development store, where there is no limit.
Theme and checkout trouble is the recurring complaint. Below Premium on Shopify Plus, the date and slot picker lives on the cart page, not in checkout. In February 2026 a merchant wrote that the address field locked up past the cart and cost them a day of sales; the vendor replied that it had been resolved. A florist wrote in January 2026 that zip-code validation could be bypassed and that they reproduced it on the demo store, and a store with more than two years on the app wrote in July 2026 that Pickeasy breaks their checkout, while praising the support. Test the full path, cart to paid order, on a duplicate theme before you publish. Support runs 20 hours a day and is offline from 3:00 to 7:00 AM India time, according to a vendor reply from May 20

video:video.video:title: Pingtree Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two things about this price list will cost you money if you skim it. First, the $499 is a floor rather than a bill. Pingtree describes its model as usage-based and prints “overage billed after month close — no surprise mid-cycle fees” directly under the Self Service price. Leads, ping requests, clicks and database API calls past the included allowances are charged afterwards. You find out what the month cost when the month is over. No overage rate is published on the pricing page, which means the one number you most need in order to budget is the one you have to ask for. Second, the page was rebuilt between our July and August readings, and the tier structure went with it. On 27 July 2026 there were six tiers: Self Managed at Startup $499, Starter $1,250 and Growth $2,500, plus two quote-only managed tiers. On 27 August 2026 that was gone — one Self Service path from $199 a month, one Managed Services path from $2,500 — and by 1 October 2026 the Self Service floor had moved to $499. Any quote, screenshot or comparison table you were handed before October describes a price list that no longer exists, so ask for the current one in writing. There is a third gap worth naming. Copilot, the prompt-driven AI agent, is what the entire homepage is built around. Yet the pricing page is written purely in infrastructure units: leads, requests, clicks, storage, API calls. It says nothing about AI usage limits, or which path gates which Copilot capability. Read the marketing and the pricing side by side and you cannot tell what $499 buys you of the feature you are being sold on. Pingtree's own partner manager answered that question for us in writing on 28 July 2026, and agreed the pricing page says it nowhere. The answer is in the section below on what the paid path actually buys. Three things he confirmed belong here rather than in a footnote. The overage rate is still not published.
