video:video.video:title: Pipedrive Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Pipedrive manages what happens after a lead enters your pipeline — it doesn't do outbound prospecting or marketing, so you'll pair it with a separate tool for that. As you scale and need sales, marketing and support data joined up, its sales-only focus starts to lean on add-ons. In our test on 21 October 2026 the trial ran on Premium, the €79-a-seat monthly plan, so list the features you used before you settle on a cheaper seat.

video:video.video:title: Positive User Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Every plan stops at 60,000 emails a year, about 5,000 a month, and the pricing page does not say what more sending costs, so a weekly newsletter to a few thousand contacts outgrows even the €499 plan. The page prints only annual prices, seats beyond the included one or two cost €69 to €199 a month each, and auto-renewal is on by default: stopping an annual plan takes notice to your account manager at least 30 days ahead, with no refund for the rest of the term. The 7-day trial is short for an automation platform. We have not used Positive User ourselves.

video:video.video:title: Quartile Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Everything about the sales motion here is a conversation. The product is sold as a platform plus a dedicated account team, and there is no self-serve entry: the only route in is Request Demo. That carries a cost which never appears on the page — you cannot size this against your ad budget before you talk to someone, and you cannot put it next to a competitor on paper. It matters more than usual in this category, because the direct peers do publish. Our own dossiers have Teikametrics at $149 a month billed annually for up to $10K in monthly ad spend, plus 3% of spend above that (read 2026-08-01), and BidX at €495 a month for its self-service Amazon tier (read 2026-08-06). Against those two, Quartile is an unknown until you have a quote in hand.
The introductory offer that used to soften this has been withdrawn. In August 2026 a referral link carried 40% off a new customer's first three months; re-read on 11 September 2026, quartile.com/partners publishes no customer discount at all — it now rewards the person making the introduction, by an amount it declines to name. So there is no published discount left to negotiate against, and the quote is the only figure in the entire transaction.
One more figure to handle carefully: the 41% average increase in ROAS on their homepage is Quartile's own number, measured by Quartile on Quartile's customers. Nobody independent has checked it and neither have we, so ask what the sample was and over what period before you let it weigh on the decision.

video:video.video:title: Rank Math Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free version is so generous that many sites never need to upgrade — PRO mainly earns its keep once you want built-in rank tracking, Content AI credits or to manage many sites. Don't pay until you hit those.

video:video.video:title: Rapid Search Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The meter is your traffic, not your searches. Rapid Search prices on monthly sessions, and its own FAQ defines a session as a visit to the store. A shopper who never touches the search box still counts. So the plan you need follows your total storefront traffic: 2,000 sessions free, 5,000 on the $14 tier, 25,000 on the $39 tier. A store with modest search use but a lot of visitors pays for headroom it does not search with.
Going over the cap does not bill you, it switches you back. The vendor's FAQ says it sends several warnings as you approach the limit, and that if you do not upgrade, search reverts to Shopify's built-in search until the limit resets with the next charge. That is more honest than a surprise overage, but it means the best month of the year is the month your search can quietly downgrade itself. Upgrade before a sale, not during it.
The two pricing pages tell different stories. The Shopify listing stops at Basic 3, $39 a month for 25,000 sessions. The vendor's pricing slider goes on to $59, $79, $129, $199 and $349 a month, and the product cap stays at 100,000 on every tier up to $199; the listing's line that it scales to 1M+ products describes only the $349 unlimited tier. The customer logos (Levi's, Skechers, alo) and the claims of 5,000+ stores and a doubled search conversion rate come from the vendor's own site and are not sourced there. We have not installed the app.

video:video.video:title: Reditus Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The advertised $99 is the annual-commitment rate — month-to-month is $149. The affiliate-marketplace listing, often the very reason teams pick Reditus, only unlocks at Scale Up: $4,788 per year, annual-only. And payout processing fees of 5% (card) or 2% (invoice) sit on top of every plan.

video:video.video:title: Reply.io Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The $89 is the Multichannel track on annual billing, and it does include LinkedIn, calls, SMS and WhatsApp — $99 month to month. The trap is the cheaper Email track: it starts at $49 for 1,000 contacts, but LinkedIn automation ($69 per account) and calls and SMS ($29) are add-ons there, so one seat with both is $147 against $89 for Multichannel. Budget the track that matches your channels, plus sending infrastructure (domains, warmup) that any cold-outreach stack needs. The platform is genuinely capable; the pricing just rewards reading this paragraph before the demo call.

video:video.video:title: SEOKart Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Every plan, free included, lists free SEO consultancy, and it is worth knowing what sits next to it. seokart.com sells a managed SEO service at $799, $1,299 and $1,949 a month (read 14 September 2026). That is a separate, optional service rather than a tier of the app, and a free consultation is the natural place for a conversation about it to start. The evidence base is decent rather than deep: 69 reviews on 12 September 2026, launched 4 June 2020, developer Activant Solutions Pvt Ltd in Jaipur. The 5.0 average hides the shape — 67 five-star reviews and two one-star, with nothing in between. Then the two limits that decide whether this is the right tool. The rank tracker checks monthly on Free and weekly on Pro and above, so it is a trend line, not a daily rank check, and 100 tracked keywords is what every Shopify plan card publishes, but that is not the ceiling: the vendor's own configurator at seokart.com/pricing sells 200 to 500 tracked keywords as a priced step, $10 a month per extra 100 on a 1,000-product store and $20 a step on a 10,000-product one (read 15 September 2026). And one-click AI optimisation writes meta titles and descriptions in bulk: that is the whole appeal. This review is researched rather than hands-on, so take the next line as general practice with any bulk AI writer and not as something we watched SEOKart produce -- budget a pass for reading what it wrote on your best-selling pages before you let Cruise Control run unattended. The app also needs access to products, store analytics and the Online Store, plus blog contributor data.

video:video.video:title: SalesTarget.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The credit numbers on the plan cards shrink once you read the help centre's price list. Unlocking an email address costs 2 credits, a phone number 5, intent data 3, and adding a lead to a list costs another credit. Growth's 2,000 credits are therefore about 660 leads a month with a verified email, or about 250 if you also want the phone number. Sending is billed the same way on a separate balance: a plain email costs 1 email credit, but an AI-personalised email written by SalesTarget's own AI costs 5, so Growth's 5,000 emails become 1,000 if every step is AI-written. Connecting your own LLM key brings that down to 2. None of this is hidden, but none of it is on the pricing page either.
The 'Super Saver' badge on the bundle is hard to check. Lead Explorer Launch ($49, 2,000 credits) plus Email Outreach Growth ($30, 5,000 emails) comes to $79 for the same allowances as the $169 All In One Growth plan. The $90 difference buys one LinkedIn automation slot and Copilot, and the LinkedIn tab showed no stand-alone price when we read it on 1 October 2026, so we cannot tell you whether the bundle actually saves money. The yearly toggle has the same problem: it says 5%, and the real discount runs from 0% to about 15% depending on the module.
Two documents disagree on how to leave. The pricing FAQ says you can cancel any time from the dashboard with no cancellation fee, while the terms say subscriptions auto-renew unless 30 days' notice is given and that partial terms are not refunded. Cancel well before the renewal date and keep a record. The 'Labor Day Sale, Limited Time Only' banner still running on 1 October is a small thing, but it is the first thing on every page. The LinkedIn side is cautious by design: the help centre starts a standard LinkedIn account at 3 connection requests a day, takes 42 days to reach 20 a day, caps it at 100 a week, and halves your daily limit if fewer than 30% of requests are accepted. We found no independent reviews we could read: there is no

video:video.video:title: Scarcity.AI Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
All three read real data, which is worth saying before anything else — the low stock counter shows inventory levels and the visitors counter reads unique visitors, live traffic and product views. Nothing here invents a number.
But the visitors counter carries two settings that shape which true number a shopper sees. It can show the counter only after a set number of views, so a quiet product simply displays nothing rather than a small figure. And the time frame is yours to set, so 'twelve people viewed this' can mean twelve in five minutes or twelve since yesterday, presented identically. Neither setting fabricates anything; together they let you present a true number that a reasonable shopper would read as something else.
That distinction is where the legal line sits. The FTC treats false urgency and scarcity as deceptive practice under section 5 of the FTC Act, and the examples in its dark-patterns guidance are close to these mechanics: a low-stock claim when stock is plentiful, or a cart-activity figure well above the real one. The test is whether a reasonable consumer would be misled about a material fact. That test does not apply to the app; it applies to how you configure it, which means the compliance question lands on your desk rather than the developer's.

video:video.video:title: Selleasy Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The meter is your whole store, not the app. Every Starter tier counts total store orders, so the free plan's 50-order ceiling is reached by any shop doing two orders a day whether or not a single upsell ever fired — and, read the other way, a 5,000-order store running one quiet bundle pays the top step of the ladder all the same. That cuts both ways and it is cheap in either direction, but it is not the meter most people assume they are signing up to.
Second, the App Store listing shows only the Starter ladder, so it reads as though $29 is the ceiling. It is not. Pro at $49 and Max at $99 exist only on logbase.io, and that is where AI recommendations at volume and checkout upsells for Shopify Plus sit — the two upgrades a growing store is most likely to want.
Third, every Starter tier says '50 free AI recommendations' with no period attached, while Pro says '1,000 AI recommendations/month' and Max says '2,500 AI recommendations/month'. The contrast in wording suggests the 50 is a one-off allowance rather than a monthly one, but neither page says so outright. Ask before you plan around it.
And treat the vendor's headline claims as claims: the 20% AOV increase and the 40,000+ brands are Logbase's own figures on its own site, with no methodology attached to either.

video:video.video:title: Seller Investigators Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Contingency pricing is the honest kind — you pay only out of money that arrived — but 25% of a recovery is not the same as 25% of a profit, and there is one question that decides whether this is worth it for you. Amazon reimburses some categories automatically, and its policies on that have changed more than once. So ask, before you sign: which of these cases would Amazon have settled on its own within the claim window, and what exactly is the 25% charged on — the gross amount recovered, or what is left after Amazon's own fees? A free audit that finds $20,000 sounds decisive until you learn how much of it was already on its way. Ask for the split, in writing, before the audit turns into an engagement.

video:video.video:title: Seller Snap Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Read the caps before you read the prices, because the caps are what you are actually buying. Two of them deserve scrutiny. First, the revenue limits — $15,000 on Starter, $30,000 on Accelerator. Until September the pricing page printed them with no period attached; we asked, and Seller Snap confirmed to us in writing on 24 Jul 2026 that both caps are calculated per month, which is how the page has printed them since ('Up to $15K/mo revenue'). That is the reading that costs you money. $15,000 a month is roughly $500 a day, so a seller who already clears that sits above Starter before signing up — and $30,000 a month puts the ceiling of Accelerator within reach of a shop doing $1,000 a day. Measure your own monthly revenue against the tier first, because the page will not do it for you. Second, the SKU limit sits at 1,000 on both of the lower tiers, so catalog growth alone — not revenue, not users — can push you up a step. And the steps are steep: leaving Accelerator for Standard means $425/month annually or $500 monthly, roughly twice what you were paying, for capacity rather than for any feature you did not already have. The cheapest door is also not quite $100: Starter is annual-billing only, so the lowest month-to-month entry into the product is $250/month. Finally, the annual Accelerator rate rose from $175 to $212 a month between our September and October readings while the monthly rate stayed at $250, so confirm the figure on the page the day you sign rather than one from a screenshot. Worth checking first, though: Amazon already includes a rule-based repricer. Automate Pricing comes with the Professional selling plan and supports rules such as Competitive Featured Offer and Competitive Lowest Price with a seller-set price floor, so if your problem is simply matching the competitive price without going below cost, test that before paying for anything. And note what sets your tier: their FAQ says pricing follows the total number of SKUs in your Seller Central ac

video:video.video:title: Sender Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The cheapest paid price only covers 500 subscribers, fewer than the 2,500 on the free plan, so the 8.01€ headline rises as soon as your list is larger; the page shows the step prices only on its slider. The 30% annual discount is for the first year and first-time users only. Prices exclude VAT. We could not read the refund terms: the terms-of-service link returned an error page on 13 October 2026. The support speed and customer figures on the pricing page are Sender's own claims. We have not used Sender ourselves.

video:video.video:title: Signitic Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The homepage sells deployment 'without going through IT', and Signitic's own help centre contradicts that on every path in. Connecting Google Workspace is possible only from the Super Admin profile, and if that admin ever changes you have to reconnect or call support. Microsoft 365 needs an Azure Active Directory administrator account. Rolling out the Outlook add-in — the fuller of the two Microsoft options — needs a Microsoft 365 Global Administrator plus the Exchange Administrator role carrying the ReadWriteMailbox permission, must not be installed by end users themselves, and can take up to 72 hours to appear in people's Outlook. Marketing does keep the keys afterwards, which is the real promise; it does not get them without IT first. The add-in also needs a Microsoft 365 Outlook licence at version 16.0.14026.20000 or later, so Outlook 2013 to 2021 and Apple Mail fall back to the Signitic agent, which pushes plain signatures instead.

video:video.video:title: Similarweb Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Similarweb does publish a price — $125 a month for one seat on annual billing, or $199 if you pay monthly. What it does not publish is anything above one seat: the business and enterprise tab carries no figure at all and routes straight to a sales call, where the number depends on what they think you can pay. So the decision splits in two. One analyst can price this today and start a trial without speaking to anyone. A team walks into a negotiation, and should walk in with a ceiling already written down — plus the two line items priced apart from the seats: 37 months of data history is an add-on, and API access is quoted separately.

video:video.video:title: Skip To Checkout Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The cart skip blinds the measurement you would use to judge it. The vendor's own help article confirms that bypassing Add To Cart and Start Checkout makes your add-to-cart rate read lower, and recommends watching overall sales trends instead — so the feature is sold on conversion while switching off the funnel that would show it. Skipping the cart also bypasses the page where shipping thresholds, discount codes and cart upsells normally work. For a free widget the permissions are broad: view and edit customers, products, store analytics, Shopify Functions and the online store, plus customer device and activity data. And because there is no paid tier there is no support contract behind it; what you get is the vendor's goodwill, which a six-year run and a 4.6 average suggest is real, but is not something you can buy more of. The app also carries at least three different names across the listing, the help centre index and its own setup article, which makes it harder to know what you are running.

video:video.video:title: Smarty Discounts Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The evidence base is thin. The app launched on 14 January 2025 and carried six reviews on 4 September 2026, all five stars; on 11 October 2026 the listing still shows six, five at five stars and one at four, and six is not a track record, and the vendor, Neezon, is a small developer in Ho Chi Minh City rather than a company with a support contract behind it. The listing is unusually candid about what that means at the bottom of the ladder: the free plan's own feature list says low support. Add to that what the app needs to do its job. The data-access panel says it reads customer data flagged as sensitive and can view and edit customers, products, discounts and the Online Store, which is the access any discount engine needs but is still broad. And because the ladder gates discount types rather than volume, the plan you land on is decided by the one rule you cannot live without: if the campaign you have in mind needs time-period scheduling or free shipping on a single rule, you are on Pro at $25.99 regardless of how few discounts you run.

video:video.video:title: Social Bar Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: This is a styling subscription, and the listing's own framing oversells it: social icons and share buttons build no trust on their own, and 'boost sales with social proof' is a claim the app has no way to support. The free plan is free in a way that will not help you, since it is restricted to development and partner stores, so any live store is on $4.99 a month or $41.88 a year for something most themes already do in the footer. The 5.0 average deserves reading rather than trusting: two of the three reviews on the listing were written after 11 and 13 minutes of use and praise setup rather than results, while the one longer-running reviewer reports that icon placement is limited and the app is tricky to figure out at first. And more than 80 platform options mainly tempts you to advertise accounts you no longer maintain.

video:video.video:title: SoftSync Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Pro stops at five team members per workspace. The sixth person does not add a sixth Pro seat; it moves the whole team to Business, which is $59 per seat a month on yearly billing instead of $29. A five-person team on Pro pays $145 a month billed yearly; the same team plus one hire pays $354 on Business, for the same product surface, since the pricing page says both paid plans carry the same core features. If your team is near that line, price the Business plan now rather than after you have moved your pipeline in.
The monthly allowances are per user and per calendar month, and on Pro they are 1,000 campaign emails, 1,000 enrichments and 1,000 AI chats, with one connected mailbox per user. A single rep running cold outreach from SoftSync can reach 1,000 campaign emails well before the month ends, and the page does not say what happens when you do, whether sending stops or an overage is charged. Ask before you plan a campaign around it.
Month-to-month billing costs about a third more than yearly: $39 against $29 on Pro, $79 against $59 on Business. There is no free plan, and the pricing page does not state a trial length; it says the checkout shows any trial terms. SoftSync's own home page says it has no integrations directory and instead gives your AI agent a way in through the API and MCP access; if your stack depends on ready-made connectors, check the specific ones on the integrations page before you commit. We found no independent buyer reviews we could read, so the only voices on the site are the testimonials SoftSync chose, most of them from founders and investors rather than daily users.

video:video.video:title: Spiky.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The number to check first is the meeting cap, not the price. Plus and Pro both stop at 30 meetings per user per month, so the step from $15 to $24 buys features, not capacity. A rep taking two calls a day passes 30 in three weeks, which pushes you to Premium at $40 — nearly triple the entry price — for volume rather than capability. Price this from your team's actual call count and you will land on the right tier; price it from the feature table and you will not.

video:video.video:title: Stackable Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The two halves of the pitch are priced five times apart. Discount stacking — order, collection and shipping discounts redeemed with a single code — is the $19.99 Growth plan, the one the listing labels 'For Non-Plus'. The checkout upsells and linked discounts the app leads with sit in the $99.99 Unlimited tier only, so a merchant who came for the upsells is reading $1,199.88 a year rather than $239.88. There is no free plan to settle whether the stacking alone lifts an order, so the seven-day trial is the entire evaluation. One more thing to check before you commit: the Website link on the listing, www.stkbl.app, now redirects to the documentation for Discount Kit — a different, pricier Optizio app — and that documentation does not mention Stackable anywhere (checked 6 September 2026). For an app that launched on 13 October 2020 and has collected 54 App Store reviews since, ask support where the current documentation lives before the trial clock starts.

video:video.video:title: Stamped Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The $798/month figure that circulates for the full suite is real, but it is a floor rather than a ceiling: that is what multi-product access costs from the 5,000-order step, and below that step you cannot buy the bundle at all — the pricing page sells Reviews on its own, $23/month at 200 orders and $99 at 1,000, and does not show Repeat or Loyalty. So the ladder has a cliff in it rather than a slope. Crossing 5,000 orders doubles Reviews from $99 to $199, and wanting a second product moves you to $798. A second storefront is another $100 a month on top, and past 20,000 orders every card turns into "Talk to Sales". Start with one product and price the step above the volume you actually expect.

video:video.video:title: Storista Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The first thing to know is how much this ladder has moved. When we first read it on 23 August 2026 the free plan stopped at 10 videos, a $15 Basic plan stopped at 50, and storista.io sold a different product altogether, an AI UGC video generator priced per render. Read again on 10 October 2026, the Shopify listing and storista.io sell the same widget, the free plan lists unlimited videos, and the paid tiers are called Starter, Growth and Scale. One older line survives: the FAQ on storista.io/pricing still says 10 videos on the free plan. If the cap matters to your plan, ask which statement governs before you build on it.
Second, read the headline against the pricing table. AI Smart Tagging is the feature the app leads its pitch with, and it appears on Growth at $49 and above. On Free and Starter you tag products to videos yourself.
Third, the rating deserves its detail. On 10 October 2026 it was 4.9 from 54 reviews: 51 five-star, two four-star and one one-star. In August the same listing showed 5.0 from 49, which was a rounding rather than a perfect record, and that is worth checking on any app whose average sits on or near the ceiling.
Finally, the data access. When we read it in August 2026 the listing stated the app views customer device and activity data and can view and edit customers, products, store analytics, custom data and Shopify admin. That is a wide grant for a widget that displays video, and it belongs in your processing register whatever you decide about the product.

video:video.video:title: Super Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: If you are on Shopify Plus, the price block on the listing is not the one you pay from — the three published tiers exclude Plus stores in their own text, and the tier that covers you is $24.99 in a help-centre article. Beyond that, this vendor moves prices without announcing it. On 24 August 2026 another Effective Apps title, TnC, carried a ladder we had verified the day before; twenty-four hours later every tier had gone up with no change to the feature lists. Treat any price for this developer that is older than the day you read it as a guess, this one included. The review base is broad and middling: 4.7 over 254 reviews on 12 September 2026, 227 of them five-star but seven at one star, on an app listed since 17 August 2020. The app reads customer device and activity data and can view and edit products, orders and the Online Store. And be honest about what it sells. Gift wrap lifts average order value at the margin, so the app has to clear $9.99 to $24.99 a month in extra gift revenue before it pays for itself — and the revenue reporting that would tell you whether it does only arrives on Pro at $19.99.

video:video.video:title: Tapita SEO Optimizer Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The price on the listing is a Shopify-Basic price, and almost nobody reads the line underneath it. The same Premium plan is $49.99 on Shopify Basic, $54.99 on Grow, $79.99 on Advanced and $109.99 on Shopify Plus, because Tapita adds $5, $30 or $60 a month on top depending on your Shopify plan. On the Business tier the spread is sevenfold, $9.99 to $69.99, and it is the single largest factor in what this app costs you. Work out which row you are on before you compare it to anything else.
The ladder also moved. On our reads of 21 August and 10 September 2026 the top tier was Pro at $39.99 a month; on 9 October 2026 it is Premium at $49.99, $10 more before any surcharge.
The second meter has no published rate at all. Business gives you 100 AI metadata credits a month and Premium 500, and beyond that the listing says only that more audit pages and more credits carry an extra charge. It does not say how much, and it does not say how many credits one product's metadata consumes. Tapita's own sister app publishes $0.06 a credit on its listing; this one publishes nothing, so you cannot price a month of AI metadata before you install.
And the free tier is a demonstration rather than a plan: 50 products for bulk alt text and file names, 30 images a day, and the SEO audit and LLMs.txt limited to basic pages.

video:video.video:title: Timesact Preorder Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The Fixed price depends on your Shopify plan, not on what you use. CORE Fixed is $23 a month for a store on Basic Shopify and $117 for a store on Shopify Plus, and the pricing page lists the same unlimited orders and the same CORE features at every level. A Plus store therefore pays five times what a Basic store pays for identical capability. Timesact says so openly, but it means the break-even point moves with your store's size: on Basic, CORE Flexible at $17 for 100 orders is cheaper than Fixed and $37 for 250 is dearer, so Fixed wins somewhere between the two; on Plus, Flexible at $107 for 1,000 orders is still cheaper than the $117 Fixed price.
Several reviewers describe checkout gaps. A two-star review from October 2025, by a store that had used the app for more than two years, says pre-orders did not work for orders placed through Shop Pay, the Buy Button or other accelerated checkout buttons. A merchant who edited their review in February 2026 wrote that the second payment on a split-payment pre-order was charged to customers on the estimated arrival date without a notification to the customer or the store; the co-founder replied publicly and said they had tried to reach the merchant. If you plan to take deposits, test the full flow, including the balance charge and the emails around it, on a test order before you launch a pre-order campaign.
The Fixed plans are labelled a limited-time deal, and the page does not say when the deal ends or what the price becomes afterwards. Yearly billing brings CORE Fixed down to $17 a month on Basic, but if you lock in a year, ask in writing whether the price holds at renewal.

video:video.video:title: TnC Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Start with the badge at the top of the listing, because it is the one thing on this page that misleads. “Free plan available” is displayed twice, and the free plan is Development Stores — for development and partner stores only, with payment activated on upgrade. A store that takes real orders has no free tier here. It is the same shape as this developer's Blocky and TiXel listings, where the advertised free plan is also development stores rather than a working free tier, so read it as a house pattern rather than an oversight.
Second, the App Store's pricing table is incomplete. The vendor's own help-centre article lists a Plus Plan at $19.99 a month, Shopify Plus only, and describes it as the plan that shows the checkbox in the actual checkout page. The App Store listing shows four plans and not that one. The same article answers its own hidden-fees question with “No. All pricing is transparent and listed above”, which is true of that article and not of the listing most buyers will read first. If you are on Plus and you want consent captured in checkout rather than in the cart, the price is nearly three times the headline.
Third, the feature that makes the app defensible costs extra, and what it costs is not stable. Basic at $6.99 shows the checkbox; it does not record when anyone ticked it. Consent-date logging starts on Advanced at $10.99. Across our three readings the step from checkbox to audit trail has been $3, then $5, and is now $4, with identical feature lists every time and no note on the listing about any of the changes. For an app whose pitch is chargebacks and legal risk, an audit trail as a paid upgrade is worth knowing before you compare $6.99 against anything else.
Fourth, be clear about what this can and cannot enforce. On a store that is not on Shopify Plus the checkbox lives in the cart and on express-checkout buttons, not inside Shopify's checkout, because Shopify does not open that page to apps below Plus. The listing is honest about the sur

video:video.video:title: Track123 Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The overage is the most expensive order on the ladder. In-plan, Growth works out at 3 cents an order ($9 for 300), and the rate falls as you climb, to about 1.8 cents at 10,000 orders and 1.2 cents at 50,000. On monthly billing every order past your allowance costs 5 cents, and the plan does not stop you at the limit. A merchant wrote in September 2025 that the $9 plan had cost them $46 in a single month without warning; Track123 replied that the store had kept syncing orders past its 300 and advised setting the capped amount for usage charges to $0.01, or whatever figure you are willing to pay. Do that on the first day, not after the first invoice.
Annual billing swaps the surprise bill for a silent stop. The pricing article says annual plans have no overage: once the allowance is used up, new orders stop syncing until you upgrade, and the free plan stops the same way until the next cycle. The FAQ adds that after an upgrade only the last 7 days of orders sync again automatically; older ones need a manual sync, and a customer who looks up an unsynced order is told it cannot be found. On a tracking page whose job is to stop 'where is my order' emails, a stalled sync produces exactly those emails.
The features most stores would pay for sit on the $49 tier. Estimated delivery dates, automatic translation of carrier scans, removal of the Track123 branding and the Klaviyo, Omnisend, Slack and Gorgias integrations are all Advanced; Growth at $9 adds custom email notifications, PayPal and Stripe tracking sync, data export and analytics. The critical reviews are about data quality: in April 2026 a US merchant said a UPS parcel due that day showed an arrival more than a week out, and another said the auto-translation had changed a state abbreviation, which Track123 replied it had fixed. The FAQ also warns that a fulfilment app with permission to edit tracking links can overwrite Track123's link with its own. The help centre counts 1,500+ carriers and the vendor's homepage

video:video.video:title: Uniqode Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The tier jumps are steep and a lot is gated: analytics are capped at 60 days on the entry plan, scan limits apply across all tiers, and custom domains sit behind higher pricing. It's a real QR platform — but overkill if you just want the occasional code.

video:video.video:title: Upsell & Cross Sell - AW Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The meter is recommendation clicks, and the free plan's 50 a month runs out on almost any live store, with the app's branding shown until you pay. The full set of 8 placements, including checkout, thank-you and post-purchase pages, starts on the $49.99 plan; the $29.99 plan stops at 3. The developer page prices extra clicks on the entry plan at $0.012 each but showed no amounts for its higher tiers when we read it, and the listing does not say whether checkout placement needs Shopify Plus. We have not used the app ourselves.

video:video.video:title: UserTrail Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The session allowance is shared across all websites on a plan, and when it runs out tracking pauses until the monthly refill, so a traffic spike can end your recordings for the rest of the month. Lower plans also cap a single recording at 5 or 10 minutes and keep data for 1 or 6 months. UserTrail is a young product with little public track record, and monthly billing costs about 20% more than the yearly price. We have not used UserTrail ourselves.

video:video.video:title: Vendoo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free trial needs a card and turns into a paid plan on day 14, and once billed the charge is non-refundable on monthly and annual plans alike. Annual plans cannot be changed until the cycle ends. Starter includes no background removals, and automatic offers and marketplace sharing for Poshmark, Depop and Grailed are only on the $49.99-$59.99 Pro plan. UK visitors get a different, item-capped plan set in pounds. We have not used Vendoo ourselves.

video:video.video:title: Vify Order Printer Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Free only reaches your 50 latest orders and keeps Vify's branding; unlimited orders and automatic invoice emails start on the $10.99 Starter plan, and invoices from your own sender address on the $29.99 Premium plan. The listing advertises Peppol, ZUGFeRD and Factur-X e-invoicing and B2B VAT numbers without saying which plan includes them, and the developer API on the $69.99 plan is still listed as coming soon. We have not used the app ourselves.

video:video.video:title: VyReel Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The meter is clicks, and nobody says what happens when you run out. Every tier is sized on storefront clicks a month — 500 free, 10,000 on Basic, 30,000 on Growth, 75,000 on Pro — alongside a cap on uploaded videos. Neither the Shopify listing nor the vendor's own pricing section says whether the reels stop, degrade or trigger a charge when a busy month crosses the line, and no overage rate is published. The better your videos work, the faster you use the allowance, so ask support what happens at the cap before a sale weekend answers the question for you.
The track record is three months long. The app launched on the Shopify App Store on 19 June 2026, and its seven reviews, all five stars, were written between 20 June and 23 July 2026, each after anything from about an hour to 21 days of use. Five of the seven reviewing stores are in Pakistan. A 5.0 from seven early reviews tells you the setup is quick; it does not tell you how the app behaves at 50,000 clicks a month or after a year of theme updates.
The two pricing pages do not match. The listing stops at Pro, $79 a month; the vendor's own site adds Scale at $129 and Enterprise at $199, and reserves its advanced AI tagging for those two. The attribution panel on the vendor's homepage ($48,210 attributed revenue, 3.1x ROAS on video) names no customer and reads as an illustration, not a reported result.

video:video.video:title: Warn Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The app is called Warn: Warnings Checkout Blocks, and blocking checkout is the one thing most readers of this listing cannot buy at the advertised price. Checkout blocking, and showing a warning on the Checkout page at all, sits on the Plus Plan at $12.99 a month — and that plan says, in the App Store's own words, that it is for Shopify Plus stores. The $6.99 Premium plan says the opposite: for all stores except Shopify Plus. So the two tiers are not a small ladder and a big one, they are two different audiences, and which one you may buy is decided by your Shopify subscription rather than by how much warning you need. If you are on a standard Shopify plan and came here to stop a checkout, read the plan labels before you install.
The second thing to be clear about is what the app does and does not take off your hands. It renders the notice, targets it by product, collection or country, and styles it to your store. It does not tell you what Proposition 65, a GDPR withdrawal notice or an age-verification disclaimer has to say in your jurisdiction, and it does not keep that wording current when the rule changes. The compliance language stays your problem and your liability; this is the display layer for it.

video:video.video:title: folk Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: One gap has closed and one has narrowed. folk now has a mobile app — the pricing table carries a Mobile app row ticked on all three plans — so the browser-only complaint is out of date. Automation is still uneven, but the picture moved in September: Zapier and Make stay Premium and Enterprise only, and so does the REST API, yet the table now carries an MCP row ticked on all three plans. Standard therefore does have a programmatic route — through an AI client rather than a workflow builder — and no plan shows a native multi-step workflow. Enrichment is capped at 500 a month on Standard and 1,000 on Premium, and email sequences need at least Premium.

video:video.video:title: lemlist Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The per-seat plus per-email-account model makes total cost unpredictable as you scale, and reviews flag support response times and the LinkedIn Chrome-extension's reliability.

video:video.video:title: noCRM Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pitch is that salespeople hate CRMs, and the answer is a tool built around the next action rather than the form. What the plan table shows is that almost everything a sales team needs to work that way sits on the top tier. Two-way email sync is Dream at €33 a user; on Starter and on Expert, email is BCC only, which means you copy noCRM on outgoing mail and read replies elsewhere. WhatsApp lead creation and conversation sync are Dream. The VoIP integrations the homepage leads with — CloudTalk, JustCall, Aircall, power dialling, call recording, transcripts — are Dream. Roles and permissions, lead assignment, team goal tracking and team performance reports are Dream. Internal automations are Dream. noCRM's own FAQ calls Expert "the best fit for most teams", and Expert has no team management in it at all. So the honest way to read the ladder is that Starter and Expert are versions for one person — a lead list with follow-ups, and then the same thing without the caps — while the product the marketing describes starts at €33 a user a month on annual billing, or €39 monthly. That is three times the entry price, and it is the number to budget from if more than one person is selling. Two smaller things. Starter is restricted to new customers, so it is not a tier you can fall back to when a year on Expert turns out to be more than you needed. And there is no free plan behind the trial: 15 days, or 30 if you hand over a card first.

video:video.video:title: rePete Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The pricing is honest and the arithmetic still deserves care, because this is a percentage with no ceiling on it. There is no cap, no volume discount and no tier: 3% of attributed reorders at $5,000 a month is $150, at $50,000 it is $1,500, and at $200,000 it is $6,000 — for the same software. Most Shopify apps stop charging more once you pass their top tier; this one never does. If rePete works, the bill grows exactly as fast as the result, which is the deal you are signing rather than a trap, but it is the opposite shape to every subscription app you are comparing it against.
The seven-day window is where I would push back. Direct Sales at 3% requires the purchase within 24 hours of the nudge, which is a strong causal claim. Assisted Sales at 1% counts anything that lands within seven days — and a customer who buys coffee, supplements or pet food every month was going to reorder in that window anyway. You will pay 1% on a quantity of revenue that would have arrived without the message, and there is no way to tell from the outside how much. Ask for the split between direct and assisted in your first month before you judge the return.
The highest rate sits on the smallest claim. Upsells and cross-sells are 5%, charged on any extra item added beyond the reorder product — so a customer who reorders and adds one more thing pays 3% on the first and 5% on the second. That is the most expensive rate on the page attached to the action rePete has the weakest claim to have caused.
The evidence base is thin rather than bad. Nine reviews, all five-star, the visible ones from early September 2026 and describing two to three months of use. That is real usage by named stores, and it is still nine.
